🎨 Graph Coloring & Chromatic Number

TermDefinition
Proper coloringAssign colors to vertices so ADJACENT vertices always differ
Chromatic number χ(G)The MINIMUM number of colors that works
Bipartite graph2-colorable ⟺ contains NO odd cycle
📊 FIGURE — A proper 3-coloring
Adjacent vertices must get different colors. This graph contains a triangle (a–b–c), so 2 colors can never work — but 3 suffice, making the chromatic number χ = 3. The triangle is your quick lower-bound argument on the exam.
THE VALUES TO MEMORIZE
GraphχWhy
Even cycle (C₄, C₆…)2alternate two colors around
ODD cycle (C₃, C₅…)3alternation fails on the last vertex
Complete graph Kₙnevery vertex touches every other
Tree (any)2trees are bipartite
WORKED EXAMPLE — color C₄ (square) with 2 colors
VertexABCD
ColorRedBlueRedBlue
Neighbors A-B, B-C, C-D, D-A all differ ✓ → χ(C₄) = 2. For K₄: all pairs adjacent → 4 colors, no fewer.
⚠️ GREEDY BOUND
Greedy coloring never needs more than Δ + 1 colors (Δ = max degree). It's an upper bound — the true χ may be smaller.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Compute χ(K₅), the chromatic number of the complete graph on 5 vertices.
  1. 5
  2. 4
  3. 2
  4. 10
Show answer + steps
A — 5. In K₅ every vertex is adjacent to every other, so all 5 need distinct colors.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Graph coloring isn't an abstract puzzle. The same algorithm assigns radio frequencies so neighboring towers don't interfere, schedules university exams so no student has two at once, and allocates CPU registers in a compiler so two simultaneously-live variables don't collide. When you understand chromatic number, you understand all of these at once. The OA tests definitions, computation for common graph classes, and recognition of the 4-color theorem.

The core idea

A proper vertex coloring assigns a color to each vertex so that no two adjacent vertices share a color. The chromatic number χ(G) is the minimum number of colors needed.

DEFINITION
χ(G) = minimum k such that G has a proper k-coloring.

Equivalently: the smallest k for which we can partition the vertices into k independent sets.
An independent set = a set of vertices with no edges among them.

Chromatic numbers of common graphs

GraphχWhy
Empty graph (no edges)1All vertices can share one color
Tree (any tree)2Bipartite — alternate colors by depth
Bipartite graph2By definition: 2 independent parts
Even cycle C_2k2Bipartite
Odd cycle C_2k+13Not bipartite — odd cycle forces 3
Complete graph K_nnEvery vertex adjacent to every other
Complete bipartite K_{m,n}2Bipartite
Petersen graph3Famous example — 3-colorable but tricky
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — χ(C₅) = 3

5-cycle: vertices v₁ — v₂ — v₃ — v₄ — v₅ — v₁.

1
Try 2 colors. v₁ = red, v₂ = blue, v₃ = red, v₄ = blue. Now v₅ is adjacent to both v₄ (blue) and v₁ (red). No 2-color works.
2
Try 3 colors. v₁ = red, v₂ = blue, v₃ = red, v₄ = blue, v₅ = green. ✓
✓
χ(C₅) = 3. In general, χ(C_n) = 2 if n even, 3 if n odd.

The bipartite test (χ ≤ 2)

A GRAPH IS BIPARTITE ⟺ χ(G) ≤ 2 ⟺ NO ODD CYCLES
Test by 2-coloring with BFS:
  Start at any vertex. Color it 0.
  Color all unvisited neighbors 1.
  Color their unvisited neighbors 0.
  Continue alternating.
  If you ever try to color a visited neighbor with the SAME color as itself → odd cycle, NOT bipartite.

The 4-Color Theorem

4-COLOR THEOREM (Appel & Haken, 1976)
Every planar graph is 4-colorable. χ(G) ≤ 4 for any planar G.

Equivalently: any flat map can be colored with at most 4 colors so that no two countries sharing a border get the same color.

Famous for being the first major theorem proved with computer assistance.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Coloring the U.S. map
1
The U.S. is planar (drawable without edge crossings on a flat map).
2
By the 4-Color Theorem, 4 colors suffice for any state-adjacency coloring.
3
Notice: Nevada, Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona form a "ring" with all bordering each other in pairs — this fragment alone needs 3 colors.
⚠
Some maps (like Africa) need exactly 4. The theorem guarantees no planar map needs more.

Lower bounds — why χ ≥ k

CLIQUE NUMBER LOWER BOUND
Let ω(G) = clique number = size of the largest complete subgraph.
Then χ(G) ≥ ω(G) — you need at least one color per clique vertex.

Example: if your graph contains K₄ as a subgraph, then χ(G) ≥ 4.

Upper bounds — why χ ≤ k

UPPER BOUNDS ON χ
Greedy bound: χ(G) ≤ Δ(G) + 1, where Δ = max degree.
Brooks' theorem: χ(G) ≤ Δ(G), except when G is K_n or an odd cycle.
4-Color theorem: if G is planar, χ(G) ≤ 4.
5-Color theorem: easier to prove than 4-color, says planar graphs are 5-colorable.

Greedy coloring algorithm

def greedy_color(graph, ordering):
 color = {}
 for v in ordering:
 used = {color[u] for u in graph[v] if u in color}
 # Smallest unused color
 c = 0
 while c in used: c += 1
 color[v] = c
 return color
★ KEY INSIGHT

The number of colors greedy uses depends on vertex ORDERING. A bad ordering can waste colors. The Welsh-Powell heuristic orders vertices by descending degree, which often gives near-optimal results.

Greedy is NOT optimal in general — finding χ exactly is NP-hard.

Real-world applications

WHERE GRAPH COLORING APPEARS
Exam scheduling: vertex = course, edge = "shares a student". Colors = time slots.
Register allocation (compilers): vertex = variable, edge = "live simultaneously". Colors = CPU registers.
Frequency assignment: vertex = transmitter, edge = "interferes with". Colors = frequencies.
Sudoku: a 9-coloring problem on a specific graph (cells, with edges for same row/col/box).
Map coloring: the original motivation for the 4-color problem.
Conflict resolution: any "two things must differ" constraint.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Exam scheduling

5 courses; edges show shared students:

CS101—Math (shared), CS101—Phys (shared), Math—Bio (shared), Phys—Bio (shared), Bio—Chem (shared).

1
Notice CS101—Math—Bio—Phys—CS101 forms a 4-cycle. Plus Bio—Chem is a pendant.
2
4-cycle is even → bipartite → χ = 2 for that part. Plus Chem just needs ≠ Bio.
3
Slot A: CS101, Bio. Slot B: Math, Phys, Chem. Two time slots suffice!
✓
The chromatic number told us how few exam slots we need without conflicts.

Edge coloring (briefly)

Edge coloring assigns colors to EDGES so no two edges sharing a vertex have the same color. The chromatic index χ'(G) is the minimum.

VIZING'S THEOREM
χ'(G) ∈ {Δ(G), Δ(G) + 1} for any simple graph.
Always equal to one of just two values — remarkably tight.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing χ (vertex coloring) with χ' (edge coloring). They're different invariants.

Saying χ(K_n) = n − 1. It's n: every pair is adjacent, so you need n different colors.

Forgetting that "tree" includes ALL trees, not just binary trees. Any tree is 2-colorable.

Misapplying the 4-Color Theorem to non-planar graphs. K₅ has χ = 5; it's not planar.

Thinking greedy coloring achieves χ. It often doesn't — finding χ is NP-hard in general.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"χ(K_5) = ?" → 5. (K_n always needs n colors.)

"χ(C_7) = ?" → 3. (Odd cycle.)

"χ(any tree) = ?" → 2 (or 1 if no edges).

"What does the 4-Color Theorem say?" → every planar graph is 4-colorable.

"What's a clique in graph coloring?" → a complete subgraph. χ ≥ clique size.

"Real-world coloring application?" → exam scheduling, register allocation, frequency assignment.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • χ(G) = minimum colors for proper vertex coloring
  • Equivalent to partitioning vertices into independent sets
  • χ ≥ ω (clique number is a lower bound)
  • χ ≤ Δ + 1 always (greedy bound); χ ≤ Δ except K_n / odd cycles (Brooks)
  • Tree: χ = 2. Bipartite: χ ≤ 2. Odd cycle: χ = 3. K_n: χ = n.
  • 4-Color Theorem: any planar graph is 4-colorable
  • Greedy coloring is NOT optimal; computing χ is NP-hard
  • Real uses: scheduling, register allocation, frequency assignment
🧠 MEMORY AID

Chromatic number χ(G) = fewest colors so adjacent vertices differ. A graph is bipartite ⇔ 2-colorable ⇔ no odd cycle. K_n needs n colors. An even cycle needs 2; an odd cycle needs 3.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Chromatic number χ(G) = fewest colors so no two adjacent vertices share a color. χ(complete graph Kₙ) = n; bipartite → χ = 2; any planar graph → χ ≤ 4 (Four Color Theorem). OA: compute χ for a small graph.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
triangle K3: every pair adjacent -> need 3 colors
chi(K3) = 3

Result: χ(K₃) = 3

Adjacent vertices need distinct colors; a triangle forces 3. Knowing χ for Kₙ, cycles (2 if even, 3 if odd), and bipartite graphs covers most items.

📖 Learn it step by step — Planar Graphs & Euler’s Formula

A graph is planar if you can draw it on paper without any edges crossing. (You’re allowed to bend and reroute edges — the question is whether a crossing-free drawing exists at all.) When one does, Euler’s formula ties together the dots, lines, and the regions they carve out.

📊 FIGURE — Euler’s formula on a planar drawing of K4
Drawn without crossings, K4 has V = 4 vertices, E = 6 edges, and F = 4 faces (three inner triangles PLUS the unbounded outer face — always count it!). Check: V − E + F = 4 − 6 + 4 = 2, as Euler’s formula demands for every connected planar graph.
EULER’S FORMULA (the one equation)
For any connected planar graph drawn without crossings: V − E + F = 2, where V = vertices, E = edges, and F = faces (regions), including the one big outer region. Always remember to count that outer face.
TESTS FOR NON-PLANARITY
• Edge bound: a simple connected planar graph with V ≥ 3 has E ≤ 3V − 6. If a graph breaks this, it is not planar.
• Two famous non-planar graphs: K₅ (5 vertices all connected) and K₃,₃ (the “three utilities” graph). Kuratowski’s theorem: a graph is non-planar exactly when it contains one of these hiding inside it.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — find the number of faces
A connected planar graph has V = 6 vertices and E = 9 edges. By Euler: F = 2 − V + E = 2 − 6 + 9 = 5 faces (four inner regions plus the outer one).
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — prove K₅ is not planar
K₅ has V = 5 and E = 10 (every pair of 5 vertices joined: 5·4/2 = 10). Check the bound: 3V − 6 = 3·5 − 6 = 9. But E = 10 > 9, so the bound is violated → K₅ is not planar.
⚠️ COUNT THE OUTER FACE
The single most common Euler-formula mistake is forgetting the unbounded outer region as a face. And the E ≤ 3V − 6 bound only disproves planarity when broken — passing it doesn’t guarantee planar (K₃,₃ passes the count yet is non-planar).
🎯 QUICK CHECK
A connected planar graph has 8 vertices and 12 edges. How many faces?
  1. 6
  2. 4
  3. 2
Show answer
A — 6. F = 2 − V + E = 2 − 8 + 12 = 6.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A planar graph is one you can draw on paper without edges crossing — the same property that makes maps colorable with 4 colors and makes circuit boards routable. The crowning result is Euler's formula: V − E + F = 2, which links three counts (vertices, edges, faces) of every connected planar graph. With it you can prove a graph is non-planar with arithmetic alone, no drawing required. The OA tests the formula, the K₅ / K₃,₃ obstruction, and the planar bounds derived from Euler.

What "planar" means

A graph is planar if it can be drawn in the plane such that no two edges cross (except at their shared endpoints). The drawing itself is called a planar embedding.

FACES OF A PLANAR EMBEDDING
A planar embedding partitions the plane into faces: connected regions bounded by edges.

Always count the outer (unbounded) face too. So even a single triangle has 2 faces (the inside and the outside).

Euler's formula

EULER'S FORMULA
For any connected planar graph:
  V − E + F = 2
where V = vertices, E = edges, F = faces (including the outer face).

For a planar graph with c connected components: V − E + F = 1 + c.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Verify on a triangle
1
Triangle has V = 3, E = 3.
2
Inside region + outside region → F = 2.
3
V − E + F = 3 − 3 + 2 = 2. ✓
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Cube graph

A cube has 8 vertices, 12 edges. How many faces?

1
Cube is planar (project onto plane). V = 8, E = 12.
2
Euler: F = 2 − V + E = 2 − 8 + 12 = 6.
✓
6 faces — matches the geometric cube (5 sides + outer face when projected).

Planar bounds

EDGE BOUND FOR SIMPLE PLANAR GRAPHS
If V ≥ 3, then E ≤ 3V − 6.

Derivation: each face is bounded by at least 3 edges, each edge bounds at most 2 faces. So 2E ≥ 3F, i.e. F ≤ 2E/3. Substitute into Euler: V − E + 2E/3 ≥ 2 → E ≤ 3V − 6.
BIPARTITE PLANAR EDGE BOUND
If V ≥ 3 and the graph is bipartite (no odd cycles, so smallest cycle has length ≥ 4):
  E ≤ 2V − 4

K₅ and K₃,₃ — the canonical non-planar graphs

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — K₅ is not planar
1
K₅ has V = 5, E = C(5,2) = 10.
2
Planar bound: E ≤ 3V − 6 = 3(5) − 6 = 9.
3
10 > 9 → violates the bound → K₅ is NOT planar.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — K₃,₃ is not planar
1
K₃,₃ is bipartite. V = 6, E = 9.
2
Bipartite planar bound: E ≤ 2V − 4 = 12 − 4 = 8.
3
9 > 8 → violates → K₃,₃ is NOT planar.
⚠
Note the standard E ≤ 3V − 6 = 12 doesn't catch K₃,₃ since 9 ≤ 12. The bipartite bound is tighter and necessary.

Kuratowski's and Wagner's theorems

KURATOWSKI'S THEOREM (1930)
A graph is planar if and only if it contains no subdivision of K₅ or K₃,₃.

A subdivision = take a graph and insert any number of degree-2 vertices on its edges.
WAGNER'S THEOREM (1937)
A graph is planar iff it contains no K₅ or K₃,₃ as a minor.

A minor = obtained by deleting vertices/edges and contracting edges.

These two theorems give EXACT characterizations of planarity. Computer algorithms can test planarity in O(V) time using these structural ideas.

Fáry's theorem

FÁRY'S THEOREM (1948)
Every planar graph has a planar embedding using only straight-line edges.

You don't need curves to draw a planar graph without crossings.

Maximal planar graphs (triangulations)

A planar graph is maximal planar if you can't add any more edges without losing planarity. Such graphs satisfy E = 3V − 6 exactly, and every face (including the outer one) is a triangle. They're also called plane triangulations.

Genus — when planar isn't enough

GENUS
A graph that's not planar might still embed without crossings on a more complex surface (a torus, double torus, ...).

The genus g of a graph is the minimum number of "handles" needed:
  Sphere (genus 0) = plane = planar graphs.
  Torus (genus 1) — K₅ and K₃,₃ embed here without crossings.
  K₇ has genus 1; K₈ has genus 2.

Generalized Euler formula: V − E + F = 2 − 2g.

Why planarity matters

REAL-WORLD APPLICATIONS
Circuit boards: planar graphs route on a single layer.
Chip design: minimize crossings to reduce wire layers (cost).
Map coloring: planar graphs need at most 4 colors (4-Color Theorem).
Algorithm speed: many NP-hard problems become polynomial on planar graphs.
Network visualization: planar layouts are easier to read.
Roadmaps: nearly planar (overpasses are the rare exceptions).

Quick planarity checklist

SHORTCUT TESTS
✗ Has > 3V − 6 edges (V ≥ 3) → NOT planar.
✗ Bipartite with > 2V − 4 edges (V ≥ 3) → NOT planar.
✗ Contains K₅ or K₃,₃ subdivision → NOT planar.
✓ Tree (any tree) → planar (E = V − 1, well under bound).
✓ Cycle → planar.
✓ Outerplanar (all vertices on the outer face) → planar.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting to count the OUTER face. A triangle has F = 2, not 1.

Applying E ≤ 3V − 6 without checking V ≥ 3. For V < 3 it doesn't apply.

Using E ≤ 3V − 6 to test bipartite graphs — use the tighter E ≤ 2V − 4 instead.

Confusing minor and subdivision in Kuratowski/Wagner. Subdivisions add degree-2 vertices; minors also allow contraction.

Saying K₅ has 5 edges. C(5, 2) = 10.

Thinking "planar" means "drawn without crossings in the current picture." It means there EXISTS such a drawing.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"State Euler's formula" → V − E + F = 2 (connected planar).

"How many faces in a planar graph with V=10, E=15?" → F = 2 − V + E = 7.

"Is K₅ planar?" → No (10 edges > 9 = 3V−6).

"Is K₃,₃ planar?" → No (9 edges > 8 = 2V−4 bipartite bound).

"Kuratowski says..." → planar iff no K₅ or K₃,₃ subdivision.

"What's a face?" → a region bounded by edges in a planar embedding (including the outer one).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Planar = drawable without edge crossings
  • Euler's formula: V − E + F = 2 (connected planar; counts outer face)
  • Edge bound: E ≤ 3V − 6 (V ≥ 3); bipartite: E ≤ 2V − 4
  • K₅ and K₃,₃ are the canonical non-planar graphs
  • Kuratowski: planar iff no subdivision of K₅ or K₃,₃
  • Wagner: planar iff no K₅ or K₃,₃ minor
  • Fáry: planar graphs have straight-line embeddings
  • Maximal planar = triangulation, achieves E = 3V − 6 exactly
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Euler's formula for connected planar graphs: V − E + F = 2 (F counts the outer face). Used to test planarity and count faces/edges. OA: plug into V−E+F=2 to solve for the missing quantity.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
connected planar graph: V=6, E=9
F = 2 - V + E = 2 - 6 + 9 = 5

Result: F = 5 faces

V−E+F=2 links a planar graph's vertices, edges, and faces; the OA gives two and asks the third, or uses E ≤ 3V−6 to rule out planarity.

📚 Extra review — 1 alternate explanation & recall cards (tap to open)

🗺️ Planarity & Euler's Formula

TermDefinition
Planar graphCan be drawn with NO edges crossing
FaceA region the drawing divides the plane into (the outside counts as one!)
EULER'S FORMULA (connected planar graph)
v − e + f = 2
WORKED EXAMPLE — the cube graph
CountValue
vertices v8
edges e12
faces f6
Check: 8 − 12 + 6 = 2 ✓. Given any two of v, e, f — solve for the third.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — find f
Connected planar graph with v = 7, e = 10: f = 2 − v + e = 2 − 7 + 10 = 5 faces.
PLANARITY TESTS
Simple planar with v ≥ 3: e ≤ 3v − 6. The two famous NON-planar graphs: K₅ (e=10 > 3·5−6=9) and K₃,₃. Kuratowski: a graph is non-planar ⟺ it contains a K₅ or K₃,₃ "shape" inside it.
⚠️ DON'T FORGET THE OUTER FACE
A triangle drawn on paper has f = 2: the inside AND the unbounded outside region.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
A connected planar graph has 6 vertices and 9 edges. How many faces?
  1. 5
  2. 4
  3. 3
  4. 7
Show answer + steps
A — 5. f = 2 − v + e = 2 − 6 + 9 = 5.

📖 Learn it step by step — Eulerian vs Hamiltonian (edges vs vertices, again)

Two ways to tour a graph, and the exam loves testing whether you can tell them apart. The trick is one word: Euler is about EDGES, Hamilton is about VERTICES.

THE DEFINITIONS + THE EULER TEST
• Eulerian circuit = a closed tour using every edge exactly once. Test: the graph is connected and every vertex has even degree.
• Eulerian path (open, not closed): exists when exactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree. (If 2 odd, the path must start at one and end at the other.)
• Hamiltonian circuit = a closed tour visiting every vertex exactly once. There is no simple degree test — deciding it is NP-hard in general.
🔎 SEE IT — the Euler test at a glance
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — Euler by counting odd vertices
A graph’s degrees are 2, 2, 2, 2 (all even) and it’s connected → Eulerian circuit exists. If instead degrees were 2, 3, 3, 2 (two odd vertices), no Euler circuit, but an Euler path exists starting/ending at the two odd-degree vertices.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — a Hamiltonian sanity idea
For Hamilton there’s only a helpful sufficient hint (Dirac’s condition): if every vertex has degree ≥ n/2 (n = number of vertices), a Hamiltonian circuit is guaranteed. But failing it doesn’t mean “no” — you often must just search.
⚠️ EULER = EVEN DEGREES; HAMILTON HAS NO EASY TEST
Don’t invent a degree rule for Hamiltonian circuits — there isn’t a clean one. The counting shortcut (all-even → Euler circuit; exactly two odd → Euler path) applies only to Eulerian questions.
📊 FIGURE — Euler circuit vs. Hamiltonian cycle
Euler = travel every EDGE exactly once (possible iff every vertex has even degree). Hamiltonian = visit every VERTEX exactly once. They are different questions about the same graph: left, the numbered edges form an Euler circuit; right, the green cycle is Hamiltonian.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
A connected graph has exactly two odd-degree vertices. It has:
  1. An Eulerian path but not an Eulerian circuit
  2. An Eulerian circuit
  3. Neither
Show answer
A. Exactly two odd vertices → an Euler path (start at one odd vertex, end at the other). A circuit would need all vertices even.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Two famous walking problems on graphs sound nearly identical but couldn't be more different in difficulty. Eulerian = walk every edge exactly once. Hamiltonian = visit every vertex exactly once. Eulerian has a clean degree-based characterization (any algorithmist can solve it in linear time). Hamiltonian is NP-complete — no known efficient algorithm. The OA tests both criteria and the historical context (Königsberg bridges).

Definitions

EULERIAN — TRAVERSE EDGES
Euler walk (trail): a walk using EVERY EDGE exactly once.
Euler circuit: an Euler walk that starts and ends at the same vertex.
HAMILTONIAN — VISIT VERTICES
Hamilton path: a path visiting EVERY VERTEX exactly once.
Hamilton cycle: a cycle visiting every vertex exactly once and returning to start.

The Königsberg bridges (Euler, 1736)

Königsberg had 7 bridges connecting 4 land masses. Citizens debated: can you walk through town crossing every bridge exactly once?

Euler proved no, and his proof birthed graph theory:

EULER'S CHARACTERIZATION
A connected graph has an Euler CIRCUIT ⟺ every vertex has even degree.

A connected graph has an Euler PATH (but not circuit) ⟺ exactly 2 vertices have odd degree (the path starts at one, ends at the other).

The Königsberg graph has all 4 vertices with odd degree → no Euler walk possible. Done.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Test Euler conditions

Graph A: vertices have degrees 2, 2, 4, 4, 2.

1
All even → Euler CIRCUIT exists.

Graph B: degrees 2, 3, 4, 3, 2.

2
Two odd-degree vertices → Euler PATH (between them), no circuit.

Graph C: degrees 3, 3, 3, 3.

3
Four odd-degree vertices → no Euler path or circuit.

Why does it work?

Intuition: every time you visit a vertex along the walk, you use 2 edges (one in, one out) — except possibly at the endpoints. So every interior vertex has even degree. If start = end (circuit), even ALL vertices need even degree. If start ≠ end, exactly the two endpoints have odd degree.

Hierholzer's algorithm — finding Euler circuits in O(E)

def euler_circuit(graph, start):
 stack = [start]
 circuit = []
 while stack:
 v = stack[-1]
 if graph[v]: # unused edge from v exists
 u = graph[v].pop()
 graph[u].remove(v)
 stack.append(u)
 else:
 circuit.append(stack.pop())
 return list(reversed(circuit))

Linear in number of edges. The algorithm walks until stuck, then "splices in" sub-tours from any unused edges encountered. Standard introduction to constructive graph algorithms.

Hamilton — the hard cousin

⚠ NO CLEAN CHARACTERIZATION

Determining whether a graph has a Hamilton cycle is NP-complete. There's no known polynomial algorithm and no simple "count something" criterion like Euler's degrees.

This places Hamilton among the hardest classical problems in computer science.

Sufficient conditions (one-way only)

While there's no exact characterization, several sufficient conditions GUARANTEE a Hamilton cycle:

DIRAC'S THEOREM (1952)
If every vertex has degree ≥ n/2 (where n = |V|, n ≥ 3), then G has a Hamilton cycle.
ORE'S THEOREM (1960)
If for every pair of non-adjacent vertices u, v: deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n, then G has a Hamilton cycle.

Generalizes Dirac (if min degree ≥ n/2, then any two non-adjacent vertices have summed degree ≥ n).
CHVÁTAL-ERDŐS
If connectivity κ(G) ≥ independence number α(G), then G is Hamiltonian.

These are SUFFICIENT but not necessary. A graph can be Hamiltonian without satisfying any of them.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Apply Dirac's theorem

A graph has 8 vertices, every vertex of degree ≥ 4. Does a Hamilton cycle exist?

1
n = 8. Need each degree ≥ n/2 = 4. ✓
2
Dirac → Hamilton cycle exists.

The Petersen graph — the famous counterexample

The Petersen graph (10 vertices, every vertex degree 3) has NO Hamilton cycle, despite being highly symmetric and "looking" Hamiltonian. It's a recurring example showing that local regularity doesn't force a global cycle.

Hamilton cycle = Traveling Salesman Problem

CONNECTION TO TSP
TSP: given a weighted graph, find the shortest Hamilton cycle.

Decision version: "Does a Hamilton cycle of length ≤ k exist?" — NP-complete.
Optimization version: NP-hard (you can't even tell whether a Hamilton cycle EXISTS without solving Hamilton).

Heuristics (nearest neighbor, 2-opt, branch-and-bound, simulated annealing) handle TSP in practice. The C950 PA (Parcel Service) is essentially a constrained TSP.

Eulerian vs Hamiltonian — side by side

PropertyEulerianHamiltonian
TraversesEvery EDGE onceEvery VERTEX once
CharacterizationAll even degrees (circuit) or 2 odd (path)No clean rule
ComplexityO(V + E) — easyNP-complete
AlgorithmHierholzer / FleuryBacktracking, heuristics
Example useMail carrier, snowplowTraveling salesman, scheduling

Real-world applications

EULERIAN APPLICATIONS
Chinese postman problem: find shortest closed walk covering all edges (mail delivery).
Snowplow / street sweeper routing: cover every street exactly once.
DNA sequencing: assembling fragments into Eulerian paths in de Bruijn graphs.
One-stroke drawing puzzles: classic test of Euler's criterion.
HAMILTONIAN APPLICATIONS
Traveling salesman: visit every city, minimize distance.
Genome assembly: alternative formulation as Hamilton path.
Circuit testing: visit every component once during testing.
Scheduling: process every job under precedence constraints.
Knight's tour: chessboard knight visiting every square.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing "Eulerian" (edges) with "Hamiltonian" (vertices). Memorize: Euler = Edges.

Saying "even degree implies Euler path" — actually that's "Euler CIRCUIT." The path requires EXACTLY 2 odd-degree vertices.

Applying Dirac's "min degree ≥ n/2" without n ≥ 3.

Treating Dirac/Ore as biconditionals. They're sufficient, not necessary.

Confusing TSP (optimization) with Hamilton cycle (existence). They're related but distinct.

Drawing the Königsberg graph and trying random walks — without checking degrees first, you'd fail forever.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"When does an Euler circuit exist?" → connected + all even degrees.

"When does an Euler path exist?" → connected + exactly 2 odd-degree vertices.

"State Dirac's theorem" → if min degree ≥ n/2, Hamilton cycle exists.

"State Ore's theorem" → if deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n for every non-adjacent pair, Hamilton cycle exists.

"Why doesn't Königsberg work?" → 4 vertices, all odd degree.

"Hamilton cycle complexity?" → NP-complete.

"Difference between Eulerian and Hamiltonian?" → edges vs vertices.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Euler walk: uses every edge exactly once
  • Euler circuit ⟺ connected and all even degrees
  • Euler path ⟺ connected and exactly 2 odd-degree vertices (start and end there)
  • Hierholzer's algorithm finds Euler circuit in O(E) time
  • Hamilton cycle: visits every vertex exactly once and returns
  • Hamilton is NP-complete — no efficient algorithm known
  • Dirac: min degree ≥ n/2 ⇒ Hamilton cycle
  • Ore: stronger version using sum of degrees of non-adjacent vertices
  • The Petersen graph is 3-regular but has no Hamilton cycle
🧠 MEMORY AID

Euler vs Hamilton \u2014 \u201cEuler = Edges, Hamilton = Home (vertices)\u201d. An Euler circuit uses every EDGE once ⇔ every vertex has even degree; an Euler path ⇔ exactly two odd-degree vertices. A Hamiltonian circuit visits every VERTEX once.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Eulerian = uses every EDGE once: exists as a circuit iff every vertex has even degree (a path iff exactly two odd-degree vertices). Hamiltonian = visits every VERTEX once (no simple degree test — NP-hard). OA: apply the even-degree rule.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
graph with all even-degree vertices -> Euler CIRCUIT
exactly two odd vertices -> Euler PATH (not circuit)

Result: even degrees ⇒ Eulerian circuit

Eulerian existence has a clean degree criterion; Hamiltonian does not. The classic trap is confusing edges (Euler) with vertices (Hamilton).

📖 Learn it step by step — Network Flows & Matching

A flow network is a directed graph where edges have capacities (max amount that can pass), with a source s that produces flow and a sink t that absorbs it. The classic question: what is the maximum flow you can push from s to t?

📊 FIGURE — A flow network and a cut
Each edge shows flow/capacity. Flow out of s (2+2 = 4) equals flow into t. The dashed cut separates s from t; its capacity (3 + 2 = 5) bounds any flow. Max-flow = min-cut: the best flow equals the tightest bottleneck cut.
THE KEY RULES & THEOREM
• Capacity: flow on an edge can’t exceed its capacity.
• Conservation: at every vertex except s and t, flow in = flow out (nothing is created or lost).
• A cut splits the vertices into s’s side and t’s side; its capacity is the total capacity of edges crossing from s-side to t-side.
• Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem: the maximum flow equals the capacity of the smallest cut. The bottleneck cut is the answer.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — a bottleneck
s → a (capacity 10), a → t (capacity 4). Flow into a can be 10, but only 4 can leave toward t, so max flow s→t is 4. The edge a→t is the min cut (capacity 4) — it caps everything.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — bipartite matching as a flow
“Match workers to jobs” is a max-flow problem: add a source into all workers (capacity 1 each) and a sink out of all jobs (capacity 1 each), edges worker→job where qualified. The maximum matching = the max flow. A perfect matching means every worker gets a distinct job.
⚠️ FLOW IS LIMITED BY THE SMALLEST CUT
Max flow is never bigger than any cut, so the minimum cut pins it exactly. When you’re asked for max flow, hunt for the tightest bottleneck — you don’t have to trace every path if you can spot the min cut.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
The Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem says the maximum s–t flow equals:
  1. The capacity of the minimum cut
  2. The sum of all edge capacities
  3. The number of vertices
Show answer
A. Max flow = capacity of the smallest (minimum) cut — the network’s tightest bottleneck.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Network flow models any "how much can pass through this network" question — bandwidth in a computer network, gallons-per-minute through pipes, units shipped through supply chains. The crowning result, max-flow min-cut, says the largest possible flow from source to sink equals the smallest "cut" capacity. Matching solves the related problem of pairing up two sides — assignments, marriages, jobs to workers. Together they form one of the deepest and most-applied parts of graph theory.

Flow networks

FLOW NETWORK
A directed graph G with:
  Source s: where flow originates.
  Sink t: where flow terminates.
  Capacity c(u, v) ≥ 0: how much flow each edge can carry.

A flow f assigns each edge a value 0 ≤ f(u, v) ≤ c(u, v) such that:
  Conservation: at every vertex except s and t, flow in = flow out.
  Capacity: f(u, v) ≤ c(u, v).
VALUE OF A FLOW
|f| = sum of flow leaving s = sum of flow arriving at t

Cuts

s-t CUT
A partition of vertices into (S, T) with s ∈ S, t ∈ T.
Cut capacity c(S, T) = sum of capacities of edges from S to T (one direction only).

Every flow value is ≤ every cut capacity (any flow has to pass from S to T).

Max-flow min-cut theorem

MAX-FLOW MIN-CUT (Ford & Fulkerson, 1956)
The maximum flow value equals the minimum cut capacity.

max |f| = min c(S, T)

Solving max-flow gives both: an optimal flow AND a bottleneck cut explaining why nothing larger is possible.

Ford-Fulkerson algorithm

FORD-FULKERSON IDEA
Repeatedly find an "augmenting path" from s to t in the residual graph (where capacity > current flow), then push as much flow as possible along it.
Stop when no augmenting path exists.

Variants:
  Edmonds-Karp: use BFS to find shortest augmenting path. O(V·E²).
  Dinic's algorithm: O(V²·E); on unit-capacity graphs O(E·√V).
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Bottleneck cut

A graph has source s, sink t, and a single bottleneck edge of capacity 10 (all other capacities ≥ 100).

1
Place that bottleneck edge as the cut: capacity 10.
2
By min-cut, max-flow ≤ 10.
3
Saturating that bottleneck achieves flow = 10.
✓
Max-flow = min-cut = 10.

Bipartite matching as max-flow

Many matching problems reduce cleanly to max-flow:

REDUCTION
Bipartite graph with parts A, B. Want to maximize edges where each vertex used at most once.

Build flow network:
  Source s → every vertex in A (capacity 1)
  Every vertex in B → sink t (capacity 1)
  Each edge in original graph: capacity 1, A→B direction

Max-flow = max matching size.

Matching

MATCHING DEFINITIONS
Matching M: a set of edges with no shared endpoints.
Maximum matching: largest possible M.
Perfect matching: every vertex covered by exactly one edge of M.
Maximum weight matching: M maximizing the sum of edge weights.

Hall's theorem (bipartite matching)

HALL'S MARRIAGE THEOREM (1935)
Bipartite graph with parts A and B. There's a matching covering all of A ⟺
  For every subset S ⊆ A: |N(S)| ≥ |S|
where N(S) = vertices in B adjacent to S.

In English: any group of |S| people on the A-side must collectively know at least |S| people on the B-side.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Job assignment

3 workers (A, B, C). 3 jobs (1, 2, 3). A can do {1, 2}; B can do {1}; C can do {1}.

1
Try Hall's: subset {B, C} can only do {1}. |S| = 2, |N(S)| = 1.
2
Hall's condition fails → no assignment covers all workers.
3
Maximum matching size = 2 (e.g., A→2, B→1 leaves C unmatched).

König's theorem (bipartite)

KÖNIG'S THEOREM
In bipartite graphs:
  max matching size = min vertex cover size

A vertex cover is a set of vertices such that every edge has at least one endpoint in the set.
Beautifully connects matching (edges) and covering (vertices).

The Hungarian algorithm

HUNGARIAN ALGORITHM
Solves the assignment problem: minimum-weight perfect matching in a complete bipartite graph.
Runs in O(n³).

Used for: assigning workers to tasks with cost minimization, matching servers to requests, scheduling.

Real-world applications

FLOW APPLICATIONS
Network bandwidth: maximum data rate s→t.
Pipeline capacity: oil/gas/water through a network.
Supply chain: maximum throughput of goods.
Image segmentation: foreground/background separation via min-cut.
Project scheduling: feasibility checks.
Airline scheduling: aircraft assignments to flights.
MATCHING APPLICATIONS
Marriage / dating apps: stable matching problem (Gale-Shapley).
Hospital residency match: pairs medical students with hospitals.
Job assignment: workers to tasks.
Scheduling: shifts to employees.
Online ad bidding: matching ads to impressions.
Kidney exchange: matching donor pairs.

Stable matching (briefly)

The Gale-Shapley algorithm solves a related problem: given preferences on both sides, find a matching with no "blocking pair" — no two unmatched people who'd both prefer each other to their current match. Runs in O(n²). Awarded the 2012 Nobel in Economics for its applications to medical residency matching, school choice, and kidney exchange.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting flow conservation. Inner vertices have inflow = outflow.

Counting cut edges in both directions. A cut is one-direction (S → T) only.

Confusing min CUT (capacity) with min vertex cover (vertices). Both are min-min by König for bipartite.

Applying Hall's theorem to non-bipartite graphs. It's specifically a bipartite criterion.

Mixing up matching (edges) and independent set (vertices).

Saying "every flow network has a unique max-flow." Multiple flows can achieve the maximum value.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"State max-flow min-cut" → max flow = min cut capacity.

"Hall's theorem condition?" → |N(S)| ≥ |S| for every S ⊆ A.

"König's theorem?" → max matching = min vertex cover (bipartite).

"What does Ford-Fulkerson do?" → finds augmenting paths until none exist.

"Edmonds-Karp complexity?" → O(V·E²).

"Bipartite matching as flow?" → unit-capacity edges, source to A, B to sink.

"Hungarian algorithm complexity?" → O(n³).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Flow network: directed graph with capacities, source s, sink t
  • Flow obeys capacity and conservation
  • Max-flow min-cut: max |f| = min c(S, T)
  • Ford-Fulkerson finds augmenting paths; Edmonds-Karp uses BFS (O(VE²))
  • Bipartite matching reduces to max-flow with unit capacities
  • Hall's theorem: bipartite has matching covering A ⟺ |N(S)| ≥ |S| for every S ⊆ A
  • König's theorem: in bipartite graphs, max matching = min vertex cover
  • Hungarian algorithm: O(n³) for the weighted assignment problem
  • Real uses: bandwidth, pipelines, scheduling, kidney exchange, school choice
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Max-flow / min-cut theorem: the maximum flow equals the minimum cut capacity. A matching pairs vertices with no shared endpoints; König's theorem ties max matching to min vertex cover in bipartite graphs. OA: max flow = min cut value.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
source->A(3)->sink, source->B(2)->sink
max flow = 3 + 2 = 5 = min cut

Result: max flow = min cut = 5

Any flow is bounded by every cut; the theorem says the tightest cut equals the best flow — the standard way to verify a max-flow answer.

📖 Learn it step by step — Tree Properties & Traversals (level 2)

You met trees in Discrete Math I; here we sharpen the counting facts and the traversal cost that show up in algorithm analysis.

📊 FIGURE — One tree, three traversal orders
Preorder visits root FIRST (root, left, right); inorder tucks the root in the MIDDLE (left, root, right — sorted order for a BST); postorder saves the root for LAST (left, right, root). Trace each on this tree until the three lists feel mechanical.
SHARPER TREE FACTS
• A tree on n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges and is maximally acyclic / minimally connected (add any edge → a cycle; drop any edge → disconnected).
• A tree with at least 2 vertices has at least two leaves.
• Cayley’s formula: the number of distinct labeled trees on n vertices is nn−2.
• In a full binary tree, #leaves = #internal-nodes + 1.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — Cayley’s formula
How many labeled trees on 4 vertices? nn−2 = 42 = 16. (For n = 3 it’s 31 = 3.)
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — traversal cost
Any traversal (pre/in/post-order or BFS) visits each of the n nodes once, doing constant work each, so it runs in O(n) time. The height h controls the recursion-stack depth: a balanced tree has h ≈ log₂n, a degenerate “stick” tree has h = n − 1.
⚠️ HEIGHT DRIVES SEARCH COST, NOT TRAVERSAL COST
Visiting all nodes is always O(n). But searching a binary search tree costs O(height): O(log n) when balanced, but O(n) if it degenerated into a line. Balance is what keeps BST operations fast.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
By Cayley’s formula, how many labeled trees exist on 5 vertices?
  1. 125
  2. 25
  3. 10
Show answer
A — 125. nn−2 = 53 = 125.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Trees are the most fundamental hierarchical structure in computer science. File systems, syntax trees in compilers, decision trees, search indices, organizational charts — all are trees. They're the "minimum connected" graph: any fewer edges and the graph falls apart; any more and it has a cycle. The OA tests the equivalent definitions of trees, the four standard traversals (pre-/in-/post-/level-order), and basic counting (leaves, internal nodes, height-vs-size relationships).

The five equivalent definitions of a tree

A GRAPH G WITH n VERTICES IS A TREE ⟺
1. G is connected and acyclic, OR
2. G is connected and has exactly n − 1 edges, OR
3. G is acyclic and has exactly n − 1 edges, OR
4. There's a unique path between every pair of vertices, OR
5. G is connected and removing any edge disconnects it (minimally connected).

Any one definition implies all the others. They're DIFFERENT FACES of the same structural property.

Tree terminology

CORE TERMS
Root: a designated topmost vertex (in rooted trees).
Leaf: a vertex with no children (in rooted trees) or degree 1 (in unrooted trees).
Internal node: a non-leaf vertex.
Parent / child: relationships between adjacent vertices in a rooted tree.
Sibling: vertices sharing the same parent.
Depth (of a vertex): edges from root to vertex. Root has depth 0.
Height (of a vertex): edges to the deepest descendant. Leaf has height 0.
Height (of a tree): height of the root.

Counting in trees

COUNTING IDENTITIES
Tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges.
Sum of all degrees = 2(n − 1) (each edge contributes 2).
Tree with n vertices has at least 2 leaves (n ≥ 2).

In a full binary tree (each node has 0 or 2 children) with L leaves: total nodes = 2L − 1.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Identity for full binary trees

A full binary tree has 8 leaves. How many internal nodes? Total nodes?

1
Total = 2L − 1 = 2(8) − 1 = 15.
2
Internal = 15 − 8 = 7. Equivalently, internal = L − 1 in a full binary tree.
✓
Always: a full binary tree with L leaves has L − 1 internal nodes.

Special binary tree shapes

CLASSIFICATIONS
Full: every node has 0 or 2 children (no "only child").
Complete: all levels filled except possibly last; last level filled left-to-right.
Perfect: full AND all leaves at same depth.
Balanced: heights of left/right subtrees of every node differ by ≤ 1.
Degenerate (skewed): each internal node has exactly one child — essentially a linked list.
PERFECT BINARY TREE FORMULAS
Height h. Then:
  Total nodes = 2^(h+1) − 1
  Leaves = 2^h
  Internal nodes = 2^h − 1
  Min height for n nodes = ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ − 1

The four standard traversals

Reference tree:

 4

 /  /  1 3 5 7
TraversalOrderOutput
In-order (DFS)L → Node → R1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
Pre-order (DFS)Node → L → R4, 2, 1, 3, 6, 5, 7
Post-order (DFS)L → R → Node1, 3, 2, 5, 7, 6, 4
Level-order (BFS)Top-down, left-to-right per level4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7
★ KEY INSIGHT

In-order traversal of a BST outputs values in sorted order. This is the main reason BSTs exist — you get sorted iteration in O(n) without sorting.

How to remember the order

MNEMONIC — POSITION OF "NODE" IN THE NAME
PRE-order: visit Node BEFORE recursing.
IN-order: visit Node BETWEEN left and right.
POST-order: visit Node AFTER recursing.

What each traversal is good for

Use caseBest traversal

Implementation patterns

def in_order(node):
 if node is None: return
 in_order(node.left)
 visit(node.value)
 in_order(node.right)

def pre_order(node):
 if node is None: return
 visit(node.value)
 pre_order(node.left)
 pre_order(node.right)

def post_order(node):
 if node is None: return
 post_order(node.left)
 post_order(node.right)
 visit(node.value)

# Level-order uses an explicit queue:
from collections import deque
def level_order(root):
 if not root: return
 q = deque([root])
 while q:
 node = q.popleft()
 visit(node.value)
 if node.left: q.append(node.left)
 if node.right: q.append(node.right)

Reconstruction from traversals

RECONSTRUCTION RULE
Given any TWO of {pre, in, post} traversals (with one being IN-order), you can uniquely reconstruct a binary tree.

Pre + In ✓
Post + In ✓
Pre + Post ✗ (not unique in general — needs IN-order)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reconstruct from pre + in

Pre-order: A, B, D, E, C, F. In-order: D, B, E, A, C, F.

1
Root = first of pre-order = A.
2
In in-order, A splits the list: left = {D, B, E}, right = {C, F}.
3
Recurse left: pre = B, D, E; in = D, B, E. Root B; left = D; right = E.
4
Recurse right: pre = C, F; in = C, F. Root C; right = F.
✓
Tree reconstructed:
 A
 /  B C
 /   D E F

Complexity

TRAVERSAL COMPLEXITY
Time: O(n) for all four — each node visited once.
Space: DFS recursive uses O(h) call stack (worst O(n)). BFS uses O(w) queue, where w = max width (worst ~n/2).
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing depth and height. Depth measures DOWN from root; height measures UP from leaf (or down to deepest leaf).

Confusing "complete" and "full" and "perfect." Full = 0 or 2 children. Complete = filled left-to-right. Perfect = both, all leaves same depth.

Saying "every binary tree of height h has 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes" — only PERFECT binary trees do. Others have fewer.

Trying to reconstruct from pre + post alone — not unique in general.

Forgetting that in-order on a BST is sorted (the most-tested fact).

Recursive traversal uses O(h) stack — for very deep trees, switch to iterative.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Tree with 100 vertices has how many edges?" → 99.

"Sum of degrees in a tree with n vertices?" → 2(n − 1).

"Define a tree (4 ways)" → connected acyclic; n − 1 edges; unique path between every pair; minimally connected.

"In-order of BST gives what?" → sorted order.

"Which traversal uses a queue?" → level-order (BFS).

"Reconstruct tree from pre + in" → root = first of pre; split in by root; recurse.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Tree = connected + acyclic = exactly n − 1 edges = unique path between every pair
  • Sum of degrees = 2(n − 1)
  • Full binary tree with L leaves has 2L − 1 total nodes (L − 1 internal)
  • Perfect binary tree of height h: 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes, 2^h leaves
  • Four traversals: in / pre / post / level-order
  • In-order on a BST = sorted output
  • All traversals are O(n) time
  • Pre + in (or post + in) uniquely reconstructs a tree; pre + post does not
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A tree with n vertices has exactly n−1 edges, is connected and acyclic, and has a unique path between any two vertices. Adding any edge creates a cycle; removing any disconnects it. OA: use n−1 edges to check if a graph is a tree.

edges = n - 1 = 7

Result: 8 vertices ⇒ 7 edges

📖 Learn it step by step — Spanning Trees & MST (level 2)

Deeper on minimum spanning trees: why the greedy algorithms are actually correct, and the edge rules that let you decide which edges must (or must not) be in the MST.

📊 FIGURE — Minimum spanning tree on a weighted graph
A spanning tree touches every vertex with no cycles; the MINIMUM one has the smallest total weight. Kruskal: repeatedly take the cheapest edge that does not close a cycle (green picks: 1, 2, 3 — total 6; the 4 and 5 edges would create cycles).
THE TWO CORRECTNESS RULES
• Cut property: for any way of splitting the vertices into two groups, the cheapest edge crossing the split is in some MST. (This is why Prim’s greedy choice is safe.)
• Cycle property: for any cycle, the most expensive edge on that cycle is NOT in any MST (unless tied). (This is why Kruskal safely skips cycle-closing edges.)
• If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — apply the cycle property
A triangle A–B (1), B–C (2), A–C (3). The cycle’s heaviest edge is A–C (3), so it’s excluded. MST = {A–B, B–C}, weight 3.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — Prim vs Kruskal, same answer
For distinct weights both algorithms return the identical unique MST. Prim grows one connected blob outward (cheapest edge leaving the blob); Kruskal adds globally-cheapest safe edges anywhere. Different order of choices, same final tree.
⚠️ MST MINIMIZES TOTAL WEIGHT, NOT PATH LENGTH
An MST gives the cheapest way to connect everything; it does not guarantee the shortest path between two specific vertices (that’s Dijkstra’s job). Don’t use an MST to answer “shortest route from A to B.”
🎯 QUICK CHECK
If every edge weight in a connected graph is distinct, the minimum spanning tree is:
  1. Unique
  2. Never unique
  3. Always a single path
Show answer
A — unique. Distinct weights force one and only one MST.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A spanning tree of a connected graph is "the smallest backbone that keeps everything reachable." The minimum spanning tree (MST) — the cheapest such backbone when edges have costs — solves a huge family of real-world problems: laying internet cable to all neighborhoods at minimum cost, designing electrical grids, clustering data, building network hierarchies. The OA tests both classic MST algorithms (Kruskal's and Prim's) and Cayley's formula for counting spanning trees.

Spanning trees

SPANNING TREE
A spanning tree of a connected graph G is a subgraph that:
  1. Includes every vertex of G,
  2. Is a tree (connected, acyclic), and
  3. Therefore has exactly V − 1 edges.

Every connected graph has at least one spanning tree (often many).

Cayley's formula

CAYLEY'S FORMULA (1889)
The complete graph K_n has exactly n^(n−2) distinct spanning trees.

K₂: 2^0 = 1 tree.
K₃: 3^1 = 3 trees.
K₄: 4^2 = 16 trees.
K₅: 5^3 = 125 trees.
MATRIX-TREE THEOREM (Kirchhoff)
For any connected graph: number of spanning trees = any cofactor of the Laplacian matrix.

Generalizes Cayley to arbitrary graphs. Laplacian L = D − A, where D = degree matrix, A = adjacency matrix.

Minimum spanning tree (MST)

MST
Given a connected, weighted, undirected graph, the minimum spanning tree is a spanning tree whose total edge weight is minimum.

Two famous greedy algorithms find it: Kruskal's and Prim's.

Kruskal's algorithm

KRUSKAL'S — EDGE-BASED GREEDY
1. Sort all edges by weight ascending.
2. Initialize MST as empty.
3. For each edge (u, v) in sorted order:
    If adding (u, v) wouldn't create a cycle, add it.
4. Stop when MST has V − 1 edges.

Cycle check uses Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union): cheap "are u and v already connected?" test.

Complexity: O(E log E) = O(E log V) (sorting dominates).
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Kruskal on a 5-vertex graph

Edges (sorted by weight): A-B (1), C-D (2), B-C (3), D-E (4), A-C (5), B-D (6).

1
Add A-B (1). MST = {A-B}. Components: {A,B}, {C}, {D}, {E}.
2
Add C-D (2). MST = {A-B, C-D}. Components: {A,B}, {C,D}, {E}.
3
Add B-C (3). Joins {A,B} and {C,D}. MST = {A-B, C-D, B-C}. Components: {A,B,C,D}, {E}.
4
Add D-E (4). MST = {A-B, C-D, B-C, D-E}. Components: {A,B,C,D,E}. ✓
5
Now we have V − 1 = 4 edges. Stop. Skip A-C (5) and B-D (6) — they'd create cycles anyway.
✓
Total weight: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

Prim's algorithm

PRIM'S — VERTEX-BASED GREEDY
1. Start at any vertex; mark it "in tree."
2. Repeat V − 1 times:
  Among all edges with one endpoint in the tree and one outside, pick the cheapest. Add it.
3. Done when all vertices are in the tree.

Uses a min-priority-queue (heap) of "edges crossing the cut."
Complexity: O(E log V) with binary heap; O(E + V log V) with Fibonacci heap.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Prim on the same graph, starting at A
1
Tree = {A}. Cheapest crossing edge: A-B (1). Add. Tree = {A, B}.
2
Crossing edges: B-C (3), B-D (6), A-C (5). Cheapest: B-C (3). Tree = {A, B, C}.
3
Crossing: C-D (2), B-D (6). Cheapest: C-D (2). Tree = {A, B, C, D}.
4
Crossing: D-E (4). Add. Tree = {A, B, C, D, E}.
✓
Total: 1 + 3 + 2 + 4 = 10. Same total cost as Kruskal — both find AN MST.

Kruskal vs Prim

PropertyKruskalPrim
Greedy choiceSmallest edge globallySmallest edge crossing the cut
Data structureSorted edge list + Union-FindMin-heap (priority queue)
ComplexityO(E log E)O(E log V) or O(E + V log V)
Best forSparse graphs (E small)Dense graphs (E large)
Tree always connected during run?No (multiple components)Yes (always one connected piece)

Why greedy works — the cut and cycle properties

CUT PROPERTY
For any cut (S, V−S) of the graph, the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut is in some MST.
→ Justifies Prim's: always add the cheapest edge crossing the current "tree vs not-tree" cut.
CYCLE PROPERTY
For any cycle in the graph, the maximum-weight edge in the cycle is NOT in any MST.
→ Justifies Kruskal: never adding edges that close a cycle is safe — we'd be excluding the heaviest of that cycle.

These two properties (cut + cycle) are why both greedy algorithms produce optimal results.

MST uniqueness

UNIQUENESS
If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique.
If some weights are equal, multiple MSTs may exist (all with the same total weight).

Both Kruskal and Prim find SOME MST — possibly different ones if ties exist — but always with optimal total weight.

Real-world MST applications

WHERE MST APPEARS
Network design: minimum-cost cabling to connect all locations.
Electrical grid: minimum-wire layout to power all houses.
Cluster analysis: single-linkage clustering uses MST.
Circuit design: minimum-length wire layout.
Approximation algorithms: 2-approx for metric TSP uses MST.
Image segmentation: graph-based segmentation via MST.
Phylogenetic trees: evolutionary relationships in biology.
Maze generation: random spanning trees produce mazes.

Connection to other problems

RELATED ALGORITHMS
Borůvka's algorithm: another classic MST algorithm; works in parallel.
Reverse-delete: start with all edges, repeatedly remove the heaviest edge that doesn't disconnect the graph.
Steiner tree: like MST but allowed to add extra "Steiner points" — NP-hard.
Minimum cut: dual concept — find the cheapest set of edges whose removal disconnects the graph.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting that an MST has exactly V − 1 edges — the same as ANY spanning tree.

Saying "the MST is unique" without checking weight uniqueness. Distinct weights ⇒ unique MST; equal weights may give multiple.

Using Prim without a heap — O(V²) instead of O(E log V) (acceptable for dense, slow for sparse).

Forgetting Union-Find in Kruskal — a naive cycle check is O(V) per edge, ruining the complexity.

Confusing MST with shortest-path tree. They're DIFFERENT — MST minimizes total weight; shortest-path tree minimizes distance from source to each vertex.

Applying MST to disconnected graphs without specifying it must be a "minimum spanning forest."

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"How many spanning trees does K₅ have?" → 5^(5−2) = 5³ = 125.

"Cayley's formula?" → n^(n−2) for K_n.

"Kruskal's complexity?" → O(E log E).

"Prim's complexity?" → O(E log V) with binary heap.

"Trace Kruskal's on this graph" → sort edges, add greedily, skip cycles.

"Which is better for sparse graphs?" → Kruskal.

"State the cut property" → min-weight edge across any cut is in some MST.

"Is MST unique?" → yes if all weights distinct.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Spanning tree: subgraph that's a tree on all vertices (V − 1 edges)
  • Cayley's formula: K_n has n^(n−2) spanning trees
  • Matrix-tree theorem: generalizes via Laplacian cofactor
  • Kruskal: sort edges, greedily add, use Union-Find. O(E log E).
  • Prim: grow tree from a start vertex, use min-heap. O(E log V).
  • Both greedy algorithms are optimal — find an MST regardless
  • The cut property and cycle property justify the greedy correctness
  • MST is unique iff all weights are distinct
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A spanning tree connects all vertices with n−1 edges and no cycle. MST = minimum total weight. Kruskal (sort edges, add if no cycle) and Prim (grow from a vertex) both find it greedily. OA: trace Kruskal/Prim or count spanning-tree edges.

(skip any that closes a cycle) until n-1 edges

Both algorithms are greedy and optimal for MST; a spanning tree always has exactly n−1 edges — tracing edge selection is a common item.

📖 Learn it step by step — Permutations & Combinations (counting choices)

Both count “how many ways to pick k things from n.” The one question that decides which formula: does order matter? If yes → permutation. If no → combination.

📊 FIGURE — Permutation slots — then divide out order for combinations
Choosing 3 of 5 people IN ORDER fills slots 5 · 4 · 3 = 60 ways: P(5,3). If order does not matter, each group of 3 was counted 3! = 6 times, so divide: C(5,3) = 60 / 6 = 10. "Does order matter?" is the entire decision.
THE TWO FORMULAS
• Permutation (order matters): P(n, k) = n! / (n − k)!.  (arrangements — 1st, 2nd, 3rd are different roles)
• Combination (order does NOT matter): C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n − k)!).  (a group/committee — just who’s in it)
Same as permutations but divided by k! to erase the orderings you double-counted. Note C(n, k) = C(n, n−k).
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — order matters (a race)
8 runners, how many ways to award gold/silver/bronze? Order matters (gold ≠ bronze), so P(8, 3) = 8!/(8−3)! = 8·7·6 = 336.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — order doesn’t matter (a committee)
From 8 people, choose a 3-person committee (no roles). Order irrelevant, so C(8, 3) = 8!/(3!·5!) = (8·7·6)/(3·2·1) = 336/6 = 56. (Exactly the 336 from Example 1 divided by 3! = 6.)
⚠️ ASK “DOES ORDER MATTER?” FIRST
Roles, rankings, sequences, passwords, seat arrangements → permutation. Teams, committees, hands of cards, subsets → combination. Using P where you need C over-counts by a factor of k!.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
How many 5-card hands from a 52-card deck (order irrelevant)?
  1. C(52, 5)
  2. P(52, 5)
  3. 52 × 5
Show answer
A — C(52, 5). A hand is a set (order doesn’t matter), so it’s a combination = 2,598,960.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Counting problems are deceptively tricky. The single biggest source of mistakes is choosing the wrong tool: permutations vs combinations, with-repetition vs without, ordered vs unordered. Master the four cases, learn to recognize which one a problem is asking for, and counting becomes mechanical. The OA tests recognition skill more than computation — pick the right formula and the arithmetic is trivial.

The four counting cases

Order matters (Permutation)Order doesn't (Combination)
No repetitionP(n,r) = n!/(n−r)!C(n,r) = n!/(r!·(n−r)!)
With repetitionn^rC(n+r−1, r)

Permutation P(n, r) — order matters, no repeats

PERMUTATION FORMULA
P(n, r) = n × (n−1) × (n−2) × ... × (n − r + 1) = n! / (n − r)!

Number of ways to ARRANGE r items chosen from n distinct items.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Race podium

10 runners. How many ways to assign gold, silver, bronze?

1
Order matters (gold ≠ silver). No repetition (one runner per medal).
2
P(10, 3) = 10 × 9 × 8 = 720.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Arranging all items

How many ways to arrange the letters of "STAR"?

1
4 distinct letters, all used: P(4, 4) = 4! = 24.

Combination C(n, r) — order doesn't matter, no repeats

COMBINATION FORMULA
C(n, r) = n! / (r! · (n − r)!) = "n choose r"

Number of ways to CHOOSE r items from n, ignoring order.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Pick a team

10 players. How many 3-player teams?

1
Order doesn't matter (a team of {Alice, Bob, Carol} = team of {Carol, Bob, Alice}).
2
C(10, 3) = 10!/(3!·7!) = (10·9·8)/(3·2·1) = 120.
⚠
Notice: 720 / 6 = 120. C(n,r) = P(n,r) / r! — divide out the r! orderings of each chosen set.

Permutations with repetition — n^r

WITH REPLACEMENT, ORDERED
Number of r-length sequences from an n-letter alphabet (repeats allowed): n^r.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — License plates

How many 6-character plates use letters A-Z (repeats allowed)?

1
Each position has 26 choices, all independent.
2
26^6 = 308,915,776.

Combinations with repetition — stars and bars

WITH REPLACEMENT, UNORDERED
Number of multisets of size r from n distinct types: C(n + r − 1, r).

Equivalently: number of ways to distribute r identical balls into n distinct bins.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Donut combos

A shop has 5 flavors of donuts. You buy 8 donuts. How many flavor combos? (Multiple of same flavor OK; doesn't matter what order you select.)

1
Multiset of size 8 from 5 types: C(5 + 8 − 1, 8) = C(12, 8).
2
C(12, 8) = C(12, 4) = (12·11·10·9)/(4·3·2·1) = 495.

Multinomial coefficients

MULTINOMIAL
Number of ways to arrange n items where there are k₁ of type 1, k₂ of type 2, ..., k_m of type m (k₁ + ... + k_m = n):

n! / (k₁! · k₂! · ... · k_m!)

Generalizes C(n, k) to more than two groups.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Arrangements of "MISSISSIPPI"
1
11 letters: 1 M, 4 I's, 4 S's, 2 P's.
2
11! / (1! · 4! · 4! · 2!) = 39,916,800 / (1 · 24 · 24 · 2) = 39,916,800 / 1,152.
3
= 34,650.

Circular arrangements

CIRCULAR ARRANGEMENTS
Number of ways to seat n people around a round table (rotations counted as the same): (n − 1)!.

If reflections also identified (e.g., a necklace flipped over): (n − 1)! / 2.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Round table

5 people at a round table. How many seatings (considering only relative position)?

1
(5 − 1)! = 4! = 24.

The "swap test" — does order matter?

SWAP TEST
Pick any two items in your selected set. Swap them. Does the result count as DIFFERENT from the original?

YES → order matters → permutation.
NO → order doesn't matter → combination.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Apply the swap test
A
"How many 3-letter passwords from A-Z?" Swap two letters → different password. → Order matters → permutation. (with rep: 26³.)
B
"How many 3-card hands from a 52-card deck?" Swap two cards → same hand. → Combination. C(52, 3).
C
"How many ways to seat 5 people at a row of 5 chairs?" Swap two seats → different seating. → Permutation. 5! = 120.

Pascal's triangle and identities

USEFUL IDENTITIES
C(n, r) = C(n, n − r) (symmetry — choose r OR leave out r)
C(n, r) = C(n−1, r−1) + C(n−1, r) (Pascal's rule)
C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1
Sum: C(n, 0) + C(n, 1) + ... + C(n, n) = 2^n

Binomial theorem

BINOMIAL THEOREM
(x + y)^n = Σ C(n, k) · x^(n−k) · y^k for k from 0 to n.

The coefficients are exactly the n-th row of Pascal's triangle.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing P and C. Always apply the swap test first.

Forgetting "with repetition" cases. Donut combos use stars-and-bars, NOT C(5, 8).

Forgetting to divide by repeated-element factorials. "MISSISSIPPI" has 11 letters, but 11! gives 4!·4!·2! times too many arrangements.

Using n! for circular arrangements. Round tables use (n − 1)!.

Computing C(n, r) by hand for large n. Use C(n, r) = C(n, n − r) when r > n/2 (smaller factorial).

Confusing "select" (combination) with "arrange" (permutation). Selecting a 3-card hand vs arranging 3 cards in a row.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"How many ways to arrange n items?" → n!.

"Number of 3-letter words from 26 letters with repetition?" → 26³.

"Number of 3-card hands from 52 cards?" → C(52, 3).

"How many ways to choose r from n?" → C(n, r) if order doesn't matter.

"How to arrange MISSISSIPPI?" → 11! / (1!·4!·4!·2!) = 34,650.

"5 around a round table?" → (5−1)! = 24.

"State binomial theorem" → (x+y)^n = Σ C(n,k) x^(n−k) y^k.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Four cases by [order matters?] × [repetition?]
  • P(n, r) = n!/(n−r)! — ordered, no repeats
  • C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!) — unordered, no repeats
  • n^r — ordered, with repeats
  • C(n+r−1, r) — unordered, with repeats (stars and bars)
  • Multinomial: n! / (k₁!·k₂!·...·k_m!) for arranging items with repeats
  • Circular: (n − 1)!
  • The "swap test" tells you whether order matters: swap two items and see if it counts differently
  • Pascal's rule: C(n, r) = C(n−1, r−1) + C(n−1, r)

Stars and bars counts ways to place k INDISTINGUISHABLE balls into n DISTINGUISHABLE boxes: C(k + n − 1, n − 1). Contrast with ordered selection: choosing a captain THEN a co-captain from 10 people is P(10, 2) = 10 × 9 = 90 — order matters because the roles differ.

🧠 MEMORY AID

Permutation vs Combination: Permutation = order matters, P(n,r) = n!/(n\u2212r)!. Combination = order doesn\u2019t, C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n\u2212r)!). Memory hook: a Committee is a Combination (no order); a Podium is a Permutation (1st/2nd/3rd).

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Permutation P(n,r)=n!/(n−r)! (order matters); Combination C(n,r)=n!/(r!(n−r)!) (order doesn't). The single biggest OA discriminator: 'arrangement/ranking/sequence' → permutation; 'group/committee/selection' → combination.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
choose 3 of 5, order matters: P(5,3)=5*4*3=60
order doesn't:            C(5,3)=10

Result: P(5,3)=60, C(5,3)=10

P counts ordered arrangements, C counts unordered selections; P(n,r)=C(n,r)·r!. Reading whether order matters decides which to use.

📖 Learn it step by step — The Pigeonhole Principle

The idea is almost silly-simple: if you put more pigeons than pigeonholes, some hole holds at least two pigeons. The skill is spotting when a problem is secretly about pigeons and holes.

📊 FIGURE — The pigeonhole principle
Five pigeons, four holes: no matter how you distribute them, some hole receives at least ⌈5/4⌉ = 2 pigeons. The exam version: with n items in k boxes, some box holds at least ⌈n/k⌉ — find the "pigeons" and the "holes" in the word problem.
THE TWO FORMS
• Basic: if n items go into m boxes and n > m, at least one box has ≥ 2 items.
• Generalized: with n items in m boxes, at least one box has ≥ ⌈n/m⌉ items (round up). This is the version most problems need.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — the classic
Among any 13 people, at least two share a birth month. Pigeons = 13 people, holes = 12 months. 13 > 12, so some month has ≥ 2 people. ✓
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — the generalized form
If 25 students are assigned to 4 project groups, some group has at least how many? ⌈25/4⌉ = ⌈6.25⌉ = 7 students. (You can’t split 25 into 4 groups all ≤ 6, since 4×6 = 24 < 25.)
⚠️ ROUND UP, AND IDENTIFY PIGEONS vs HOLES
The generalized bound uses the ceiling ⌈n/m⌉ — always round up. The hard part is modeling: decide what the “items” (pigeons) are and what the “categories” (holes) are. Guarantee is about the worst case — it says “at least,” not “exactly.”
🎯 QUICK CHECK
10 pairs of socks (20 socks) in a drawer, 5 colors. Pulling socks blindly, at least one color must repeat after how many picks (guaranteed)?
  1. 6
  2. 5
  3. 11
Show answer
A — 6. 5 colors = 5 holes; 6 socks > 5 holes forces two of the same color (⌈6/5⌉ = 2).
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The pigeonhole principle is the most surprisingly powerful idea in counting: a near-trivial observation that, applied cleverly, proves striking existence claims. Among any 13 people, two share a birth month. Among any 5 points in a unit square, two are within √2/2 of each other. Among any 8 integers, two have a difference divisible by 7. The principle itself is obvious; the art is choosing the right "pigeons" and "holes." It's a foundational tool in combinatorics, number theory, and theoretical computer science.

The basic principle

BASIC PIGEONHOLE PRINCIPLE
If you place n + 1 objects into n boxes, then at least one box contains at least 2 objects.

More generally: if more pigeons than holes, some hole has ≥ 2 pigeons.

Almost trivial as a statement. The art is in choosing the pigeons and holes so the conclusion solves a real problem.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — 13 people, shared birth month
1
Pigeons = 13 people. Holes = 12 months.
2
13 > 12 → at least two people share a birth month.
✓
Pigeonhole guarantees existence; doesn't tell us WHICH month.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Same number of friends

In any group of n ≥ 2 people, two have the same number of friends within the group.

1
Each person's friend count is in {0, 1, 2, ..., n−1} — n possible values.
2
But you can't have BOTH "0 friends" (someone with no friends) AND "n−1 friends" (someone friends with everyone, including the loner) simultaneously — contradiction.
3
So friend counts actually live in either {0, 1, ..., n−2} or {1, 2, ..., n−1} — n−1 values.
4
n people, n−1 possible counts → pigeonhole → two people share a count.

Generalized pigeonhole

GENERALIZED PIGEONHOLE
If you place N objects into k boxes, then at least one box contains at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects.

⌈x⌉ = ceiling = smallest integer ≥ x.

Special case: to guarantee at least g per box, you need N ≥ k(g − 1) + 1 objects.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Drawer of socks

A drawer has 10 red, 10 blue, 10 green socks. How many to grab to guarantee a matching pair?

1
Pigeons = socks grabbed. Holes = 3 colors.
2
Need ≥ 2 in some hole. Use formula: N ≥ k(g − 1) + 1 = 3(2 − 1) + 1 = 4.
✓
Grab 4 socks — guaranteed at least 2 of the same color.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Three of a kind

Same drawer. How many to guarantee 3 of one color?

1
g = 3 (want ≥ 3 of one color). k = 3 colors.
2
N ≥ k(g − 1) + 1 = 3(2) + 1 = 7.
✓
Grab 7 socks — guaranteed at least 3 of the same color.

Number theory applications

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Difference divisible by n

Among any n + 1 integers, two have a difference divisible by n.

1
Pigeons = n + 1 integers. Holes = n possible residues mod n: {0, 1, ..., n−1}.
2
Pigeonhole → two integers a, b have the same residue mod n.
3
Then a − b ≡ 0 (mod n), so n | (a − b).
✓
This is a number-theory cornerstone. Try it: among any 8 integers, two differ by a multiple of 7.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Subset with sum divisible by n

Given any n integers, some non-empty subset has sum divisible by n.

1
Let s_i = a_1 + a_2 + ... + a_i (partial sums) for i = 1..n.
2
Each s_i mod n is in {0, 1, ..., n − 1}.
3
If any s_i ≡ 0 (mod n), the subset {a_1, ..., a_i} works.
4
Otherwise, all n partial sums are in n − 1 residue classes → two must match: s_i ≡ s_j (mod n) for i < j.
5
Then s_j − s_i = a_{i+1} + ... + a_j ≡ 0 (mod n). The subset {a_{i+1}, ..., a_j} works.

Geometric pigeonhole

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Points in a unit square

Among any 5 points in a unit square, two are at distance ≤ √2/2.

1
Divide the unit square into 4 quadrants of side 1/2.
2
5 points, 4 quadrants → some quadrant has ≥ 2 points.
3
Diagonal of a 1/2 × 1/2 square is √(1/4 + 1/4) = √2/2 ≈ 0.707.
✓
Two points in the same quadrant are at distance ≤ √2/2.

Choosing the right pigeons and holes

COMMON HOLE CHOICES
Residues mod n — proves divisibility / common-difference results
Geometric subregions — proves close-together / overlap results
Possible outcomes of a finite process — proves repetition results
Color classes — proves Ramsey-type results (every 2-coloring of K₆ has a monochromatic triangle)
Count buckets — proves "two things have the same count"

What pigeonhole proves — and doesn't

⚠ EXISTENCE, NOT CONSTRUCTION

Pigeonhole proves SOMETHING exists with a property. It typically does NOT tell you WHICH object — only that one is guaranteed.

Example: "Two of 13 people share a birth month" — but pigeonhole doesn't say which two or which month.

This is the strength and limitation of the principle.

Ramsey-type results (a glimpse)

Pigeonhole generalizes to Ramsey theory: in any sufficiently large structure, you can always find a "patterned" sub-structure.

RAMSEY R(3,3) = 6
In any 2-coloring of the edges of K₆, there's a monochromatic triangle.

Proof sketch: pick any vertex v. It has 5 edges of 2 colors → pigeonhole says ≥ 3 are the same color (say red). If any of those 3 endpoints is red-connected to another, we have a red triangle. Otherwise all pairs among them are blue → blue triangle.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting the "+1." 12 people don't guarantee shared birth month; 13 do.

Confusing "some box has ≥ 2" with "every box has ≥ 2." Pigeonhole only guarantees AT LEAST ONE crowded box.

Mis-stating the formula. To guarantee g per box from k boxes: need N ≥ k(g−1) + 1.

Trying to use pigeonhole to find specific objects (it gives existence only).

Picking the wrong pigeons or holes. Often, your first attempt won't reveal the structure — try residues mod n, geometric partitions, or count buckets.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"How many socks to guarantee a matching pair?" → k(g−1)+1 with g=2.

"Among 13 people, prove two share a birth month" → state pigeons and holes, apply principle.

"Generalized pigeonhole formula?" → ⌈N/k⌉ minimum in some box.

"Why is this an existence proof?" → pigeonhole doesn't construct the object, just guarantees one exists.

"Among n+1 integers, what's true?" → two have a difference divisible by n.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Basic pigeonhole: n+1 objects in n boxes ⇒ some box has ≥ 2
  • Generalized: N objects in k boxes ⇒ some box has ≥ ⌈N/k⌉
  • Threshold: to guarantee g per box, need N ≥ k(g − 1) + 1
  • Pigeonhole proves existence, not construction
  • Common holes: residues mod n, geometric subregions, possible outcomes of a finite process
  • The art is choosing the right pigeons and holes
  • Generalizes to Ramsey theory — every sufficiently large structure has patterned substructure

📖 Learn it step by step — Generating Functions (turn a sequence into a polynomial)

A generating function is a clever trick: pack a whole sequence a₀, a₁, a₂, … into the coefficients of a power series a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + … Then algebra on the function answers counting questions about the sequence.

📊 FIGURE — Generating functions: coefficients do the counting
Expand (1 + x)⁴ and the coefficient of xᵏ is C(4, k) — the number of ways to pick k items from 4. Multiplying generating functions automatically handles "choose some from here AND some from there": convolution does the case-work for you.
THE ONE FORMULA THAT UNLOCKS IT
The geometric series identity is the workhorse:
  1 + x + x² + x³ + … = 1/(1 − x)  (for |x| < 1).
So the sequence 1, 1, 1, 1, … is “stored” as the tidy function 1/(1−x). Variations: 1/(1−ax) stores 1, a, a², … and 1/(1−x)² stores 1, 2, 3, 4, …
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — read coefficients as counts
The number of ways to pick a subset’s worth of coins can be modeled by multiplying factors like (1 + x). For choosing any number of 3 distinct items, (1+x)³ = 1 + 3x + 3x² + x³: the coefficient of x² is 3 = C(3,2), the number of 2-element subsets. The exponent tracks “how many chosen,” the coefficient tracks “how many ways.”
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — a making-change setup
Ways to make change with pennies and nickels: pennies contribute (1 + x + x² + …) = 1/(1−x); nickels contribute (1 + x⁵ + x¹⁰ + …) = 1/(1−x⁵). Multiply them; the coefficient of xⁿ is the number of ways to make n cents. Generating functions turn “count the ways” into “find a coefficient.”
⚠️ THE EXPONENT IS THE “AMOUNT,” THE COEFFICIENT IS THE “COUNT”
Keep the roles straight: x’s power encodes the total (size, cents, items chosen); the number in front is how many ways to reach that total. The point of the closed form 1/(1−x) is to do the bookkeeping with algebra instead of listing cases.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
The generating function for the constant sequence 1, 1, 1, 1, … is:
  1. 1/(1 − x)
  2. 1 − x
  3. x/(1 − x)
Show answer
A — 1/(1−x). That is exactly 1 + x + x² + x³ + …, all coefficients 1.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Generating functions turn counting problems into algebra. Need to count the number of ways to make change for $1.00 using pennies, nickels, dimes, and quarters? Generating functions reduce the entire question to a polynomial coefficient. Need to solve a recurrence like Fibonacci? Generating functions give you a closed-form formula. They unify combinatorics and provide a powerful general-purpose problem-solving tool.

The core idea

A generating function is a polynomial (or power series) where the COEFFICIENT of x^n encodes the count of something with size n.

DEFINITION
Given a sequence a₀, a₁, a₂, ..., its (ordinary) generating function is:
G(x) = a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + a₃x³ + ...

We treat G(x) as a FORMAL OBJECT — questions about convergence are sidestepped. The variable x is a placeholder, not a value to plug in.

Famous generating functions

CORE FORMULAS
Geometric series: 1 + x + x² + x³ + ... = 1 / (1 − x)
Finite geometric: 1 + x + x² + ... + x^n = (1 − x^(n+1)) / (1 − x)
Binomial: (1 + x)^n = Σ C(n, k) x^k
Negative binomial: 1/(1 − x)^n = Σ C(n + k − 1, k) x^k
Exponential: e^x = Σ x^k / k!

Counting subsets

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Number of subsets of {1, 2, ..., n}

Each element is either IN or OUT. The generating function for ONE element is (1 + x): "exclude (count 1) or include (contributes one to size)."

1
For n elements, multiply: (1 + x)(1 + x)...(1 + x) = (1 + x)^n.
2
Coefficient of x^k = C(n, k) — number of size-k subsets.
3
Total subsets = G(1) = 2^n. ✓

Stars and bars via generating functions

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Distribute 10 identical candies among 4 kids

Each kid can get 0, 1, 2, ... candies. The generating function for ONE kid is 1 + x + x² + ... = 1/(1 − x).

1
For 4 kids, multiply: [1/(1 − x)]^4 = 1/(1 − x)^4.
2
Coefficient of x^10 = C(10 + 4 − 1, 10) = C(13, 10) = C(13, 3) = 286.
✓
Same answer as stars-and-bars formula. Generating functions REDERIVE it.

Coin change problem

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Ways to make change for $0.10 (10¢)

Coins: penny (1¢), nickel (5¢), dime (10¢). How many combinations sum to 10¢?

1
Penny GF: 1 + x + x² + x³ + ... = 1/(1 − x). (Use any number of pennies.)
2
Nickel GF: 1 + x⁵ + x¹⁰ + ... = 1/(1 − x⁵). (Each nickel adds 5¢.)
3
Dime GF: 1 + x¹⁰ + x²⁰ + ... = 1/(1 − x¹⁰).
4
Combined GF: 1 / [(1 − x)(1 − x⁵)(1 − x¹⁰)].
5
Coefficient of x¹⁰: enumerate combos. 0 dimes + 0 nickels = 1 way (10 pennies). 0 dimes + 1 nickel = 1 way (5 pennies). 0 dimes + 2 nickels = 1 way (0 pennies). 1 dime = 1 way. Total: 4 ways.
✓
Generating functions handle change-making for any amount via coefficient extraction.

Operations on generating functions

OperationEffect on sequence
G(x) + H(x)Term-wise sum: a_n + b_n
G(x) · H(x)Convolution: c_n = Σ a_k · b_{n−k}
x · G(x)Shift right: 0, a₀, a₁, a₂, ...
G(x) / (1 − x)Partial sums: a₀, a₀+a₁, a₀+a₁+a₂, ...
G'(x)Multiply by index: a₁, 2a₂, 3a₃, ...

Solving recurrences with generating functions

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Solve a_n = 2·a_{n-1} + 1 with a₀ = 0
1
Multiply both sides by x^n and sum from n=1 to ∞: G(x) − a₀ = 2x · G(x) + x/(1 − x).
2
Substitute a₀ = 0: G(x)(1 − 2x) = x/(1 − x).
3
G(x) = x / [(1 − 2x)(1 − x)].
4
Partial fractions: G(x) = 1/(1 − 2x) − 1/(1 − x).
5
Expand each term: 1/(1 − 2x) = Σ 2^n x^n. 1/(1 − x) = Σ x^n.
✓
Coefficient of x^n: a_n = 2^n − 1. Closed-form solution!

Exponential generating functions (EGFs)

EGF DEFINITION
For sequences where order matters (permutation problems):
EGF(x) = Σ a_n · x^n / n!

Used for: counting labeled structures, exponential growth problems, Stirling numbers.

Why care about generating functions?

SUPERPOWERS
Solve recurrences in closed form (Fibonacci, Catalan, etc.)
Count combinatorial objects uniformly (subsets, partitions, change-making)
Prove identities by manipulating generating functions algebraically
Estimate asymptotics via generating function singularities
Compute moments in probability via probability generating functions
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Treating x as a number to plug in. Generating functions are FORMAL — you don't evaluate them in general.

Confusing convergence with formal manipulation. 1/(1 − x) "diverges for |x| ≥ 1" but as a formal power series it's perfectly fine.

Mixing OGF (ordinary) and EGF (exponential). Use OGF for unordered counting, EGF for labeled/ordered.

Forgetting that multiplication of GFs corresponds to CONVOLUTION of sequences (not term-wise multiplication).

Stopping at the GF instead of EXTRACTING the coefficient. The answer is the coefficient, not the GF.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"GF for the sequence 1, 1, 1, ..." → 1/(1 − x).

"GF for choosing subsets of {1, ..., n}" → (1 + x)^n.

"GF for distributing n identical items into k bins" → 1/(1 − x)^k.

"Coefficient of x^n in 1/(1 − x)^k" → C(n + k − 1, n).

"Set up GF for change-making with coins of values v₁, v₂, ..." → 1/[(1 − x^v₁)(1 − x^v₂)...].

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Generating function: G(x) = Σ a_n x^n encoding a sequence
  • Geometric: 1/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x² + ...
  • Binomial: (1 + x)^n encodes subset counts
  • Negative binomial: 1/(1 − x)^n encodes stars-and-bars
  • Multiplication of GFs ⟺ convolution of sequences
  • Coin-change: coefficient extraction in 1/[(1−x^v₁)...(1−x^v_k)]
  • Solve recurrences: convert recurrence → algebraic GF equation → partial fractions → coefficients
  • EGFs (Σ a_n x^n / n!) for ordered/labeled structures

Generating functions: the ordinary generating function (1 + x)ⁿ has coefficients C(n, k) for k = 0..n — the binomial theorem read as a power series. For exponential generating functions, eˣ generates the sequence 1, 1, 1, … (aₙ = 1 for all n), since eˣ = Σ xⁿ/n!.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A generating function encodes a sequence as coefficients of a power series; multiplying/expanding solves counting and recurrence problems. OA-level: recognize that the coefficient of xⁿ counts the ways, and know 1/(1−x)=Σxⁿ.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
1/(1-x) = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + ...
coefficient of x^n = 1 (ways)

Result: coefficient of xⁿ = count

Generating functions turn combinatorial counting into algebra on power series; extracting the xⁿ coefficient gives the count you want.
