📖 Learn it step by step — Finite Automata & Regular Expressions

A finite automaton (finite-state machine) is a tiny abstract computer: a set of states, and rules to jump between them as it reads input symbols one at a time. It accepts a string if it ends in an accepting state. Regular expressions describe the same languages.

THE PIECES
• States (circles), a start state, and one or more accepting states (double circles).
• Transitions: arrows labeled with input symbols — “in state X reading symbol a, go to state Y.”
• DFA = deterministic (exactly one move per symbol). NFA = may have choices; both recognize exactly the regular languages.
• A regular expression (using concatenation, | for OR, and * for “zero or more”) describes the same class of languages.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — what does this machine accept?
Two states: Start (accepting) and Odd. Reading a “1” flips between them; start counts 0 ones. It accepts strings with an even number of 1s. The state remembers only parity — that’s the power and the limit of finite memory.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — read a regular expression
ab* means “an a, then zero or more b’s”: matches a, ab, abb, abbb, … (the * applies to b only). (a|b)* means “any string of a’s and b’s,” including the empty string.
⚠️ FINITE MEMORY = CAN’T COUNT ARBITRARILY
Finite automata have a fixed number of states, so they can track parity or “seen so far” patterns but cannot count without bound. The language aⁿbⁿ (equal numbers of a’s then b’s) is not regular — no finite automaton can do it; you need a grammar/stack (next section).
🎯 QUICK CHECK
Finite automata recognize exactly the:
  1. Regular languages
  2. Context-free languages
  3. All languages
Show answer
A — regular languages. DFAs, NFAs, and regular expressions all describe the same class: the regular languages.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A finite automaton is the simplest computational model — a machine with finite memory (a fixed number of states) and a one-way input tape. Despite their simplicity, they're surprisingly powerful: they can recognize patterns ("does this email contain a phone number?"), validate input ("is this a well-formed identifier?"), drive lexer/tokenizer phases of every compiler, and model digital circuits' control logic. Finite automata also define exactly the regular languages — the languages describable by regular expressions. Two flavors: DFA (deterministic, exactly one transition per input symbol) and NFA (nondeterministic, may have multiple transitions or none). Surprising and important: they have the same expressive power.

Alphabets, strings, languages

FORMAL DEFINITIONS
Alphabet Σ: a finite, non-empty set of symbols (e.g., {0, 1} or {a, b, c}).
String: a finite sequence of symbols from Σ. The empty string is ε.
Σ*: the set of all strings over Σ (including ε).
Language L: a subset of Σ* — i.e., a (possibly infinite) collection of strings.

Deterministic finite automaton (DFA)

A DFA is a tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F):

DFA — FORMAL DEFINITION
Q: finite set of states.
Σ: alphabet.
δ: transition function δ: Q × Σ → Q. Exactly one next state per (current state, input symbol).
q₀ ∈ Q: the start state.
F ⊆ Q: set of accepting (final) states.

A string w ∈ Σ* is accepted by the DFA iff reading w from q₀ ends in some state in F.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A DFA accepting strings ending in "01"

Σ = {0, 1}. States Q = {q₀, q₁, q₂}. Start q₀. Accept F = {q₂}.

1
q₀: nothing useful seen. On '0': go to q₁. On '1': stay at q₀.
2
q₁: just saw '0'. On '0': stay (still saw '0' last). On '1': go to q₂ (saw "01").
3
q₂: just saw "01". On '0': go to q₁ (saw '0' again). On '1': go to q₀ (broken pattern).
✓
Trace "1101": q₀ → q₀ → q₀ → q₁ → q₂. Accepted.
📊 FIGURE — A DFA that accepts strings ending in "01"
Start at q₀ (arrow from nowhere). Read the input one symbol at a time, following labeled edges. The double circle q₂ is the accepting state: a string is accepted iff you END there. Trace "1101": q₀→q₀→q₀→q₁→q₂ ✓ accepted.

Nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA)

An NFA relaxes the DFA's "one transition" requirement: there can be multiple transitions on the same symbol, or no transitions at all, or even ε-transitions (move without consuming input). The NFA accepts a string if some sequence of choices leads to an accepting state.

NFA — FORMAL DEFINITION
Same tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) but now δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → 2^Q (set of possible next states).

Accept w iff SOME path from q₀ to some state in F reads w.

NFA = DFA in expressive power

Surprising and beautiful fact: NFAs and DFAs accept exactly the same languages. Every NFA has an equivalent DFA (and vice versa, trivially).

SUBSET CONSTRUCTION
Convert NFA to DFA: each DFA state corresponds to a SUBSET of NFA states.

Worst-case DFA size: 2^|Q_NFA| states. Common in practice: much smaller.

This is the algorithm regex engines use internally to compile patterns to fast DFAs.

Regular languages

The regular languages are exactly those accepted by some DFA. Equivalent characterizations:

REGULAR LANGUAGE — EQUIVALENT DEFINITIONS
L is regular iff:
• Some DFA accepts L.
• Some NFA accepts L.
• Some regular expression describes L.

This three-way equivalence (Kleene's theorem) is one of the foundational results of computer science.

Regular expressions

REGULAR EXPRESSION SYNTAX
∅: the empty language.
ε: the language {ε} containing only the empty string.
a: for each a ∈ Σ, the language {a}.
R + S (or R | S): union — strings in R or in S.
R · S (or RS): concatenation — strings of the form rs where r ∈ R, s ∈ S.
R*: Kleene star — zero or more concatenations of strings in R.

Standard precedence: * > · > +.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Regex examples
1
(0+1)* — all binary strings.
2
0(0+1)*1 — strings starting with 0 and ending with 1.
3
(0+1)*01 — strings ending in "01".
4
(00)* — strings of even number of 0s, no 1s.

Closure properties of regular languages

REGULAR LANGUAGES ARE CLOSED UNDER:
Union: if L₁, L₂ regular, so is L₁ ∪ L₂.
Concatenation: if L₁, L₂ regular, so is L₁ · L₂.
Kleene star: if L regular, so is L*.
Intersection: if L₁, L₂ regular, so is L₁ ∩ L₂.
Complement: if L regular, so is Σ* \\ L.
Difference, reverse, homomorphism, ... all preserved.

The pumping lemma

Some languages are NOT regular — for example, "balanced parentheses" or "the same number of 0s as 1s." The pumping lemma is the standard tool to prove non-regularity.

PUMPING LEMMA FOR REGULAR LANGUAGES
If L is regular, there exists a "pumping length" p ≥ 1 such that for any w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p, w can be split as w = xyz with:
1. |y| ≥ 1 (y is non-empty);
2. |xy| ≤ p;
3. for every i ≥ 0, x · yⁱ · z ∈ L.

To prove L is NOT regular: find w ∈ L of length ≥ p such that NO valid xyz partition allows pumping.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0} is not regular
1
Suppose L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ} is regular. Take pumping length p; consider w = 0^p · 1^p ∈ L.
2
By pumping lemma, w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1.
3
Since |xy| ≤ p, both x and y are made of 0s only. y has at least one 0.
4
Pump y twice: xy²z has more 0s than 1s. Not in L. Contradiction.
✓
Therefore L is not regular.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Thinking NFAs are more powerful than DFAs. They accept the same languages — NFAs are just easier to design.

Forgetting DFA must have a transition for EVERY (state, symbol). Missing transitions break determinism.

Confusing acceptance modes. DFA: end in F after reading w. NFA: SOME path ends in F.

Misreading regex precedence: a + b · c means a + (b·c), not (a + b)·c.

Believing all infinite languages are regular. {0ⁿ1ⁿ} is infinite but not regular.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Is L regular?" — try to give a regex or DFA. If it requires "counting" past a constant, suspect non-regular.

"DFA vs NFA expressive power?" — equivalent.

"Construct a DFA for L" — work out states based on what info you must remember.

"What is the regex for ...?" — use unions, concatenations, and Kleene stars.

"Prove L is not regular" — pumping lemma argument.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • A DFA has finite states, deterministic transitions, and an accept set.
  • An NFA allows multiple transitions and ε-moves; same expressive power as DFA.
  • Regular languages = DFA-recognizable = NFA-recognizable = regex-describable (Kleene's theorem).
  • Regular languages closed under union, concatenation, star, intersection, complement.
  • Pumping lemma: tool to prove non-regularity by finding a string that can't be pumped.
  • {0ⁿ1ⁿ} is NOT regular — finite automata can't count unboundedly.
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A DFA has exactly one transition per symbol per state (deterministic); an NFA may have several or ε-moves. Both recognize the REGULAR languages, matched by regular expressions. OA: DFA vs NFA definition, and regex ↔ finite automata equivalence.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

accepts: '', 'ab', 'abab', ...

Result: regex = DFA = NFA (regular languages)

DFAs, NFAs, and regular expressions all describe exactly the regular languages; the OA tests the determinism distinction and this equivalence.

📖 Learn it step by step — Context-Free Grammars

A context-free grammar (CFG) is a set of replacement rules that generate strings. Start from a special symbol and keep replacing until only terminal symbols remain. CFGs are more powerful than finite automata — they describe programming-language syntax.

THE PIECES OF A GRAMMAR
• Terminals = the actual symbols of the language (like a, b, or “+”).
• Non-terminals = variables (like S, A) that stand for “something to be expanded.”
• Productions = rules like S → aSb (“replace S with aSb”).
• Start symbol = where derivations begin (usually S). A string is in the language if some sequence of rule applications produces it.
WORKED EXAMPLE — generate aⁿbⁿ
Grammar: S → aSb | ε (ε = empty string).
• S → ε gives the empty string.
• S → aSb → aεb = ab.
• S → aSb → aaSbb → aabb.
Every derivation produces equal a’s then equal b’s (aⁿbⁿ) — the exact language finite automata couldn’t do. The recursion in S → aSb is what gives “matching” power.
THE CHOMSKY HIERARCHY (who’s more powerful)
Regular ⊂ Context-free ⊂ Context-sensitive ⊂ Recursively-enumerable. Each level recognizes strictly more languages. Finite automata sit at the bottom (regular); CFGs are the next step up and need a stack (a pushdown automaton) to recognize.
⚠️ CFGs CAN MATCH/NEST, REGEX CANNOT
The jump from regular to context-free is exactly the ability to handle balanced/nested structure — matching parentheses, aⁿbⁿ, nested code blocks. If a problem needs counting or nesting, it’s beyond regular expressions and needs a grammar.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
The language aⁿbⁿ (n matching a’s then b’s) is:
  1. Context-free but not regular
  2. Regular
  3. Neither
Show answer
A. It needs unbounded matching (a stack), so it’s context-free but not regular — no finite automaton can recognize it.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Regular languages and finite automata are too weak to handle anything that requires balanced nesting — like matched parentheses, HTML/XML tags, or programming language syntax. Context-free grammars (CFGs) add the missing capability: they can describe nested structures via recursion. CFGs power the parsing phase of every compiler. The corresponding machine model — the pushdown automaton (PDA) — adds a stack to a finite automaton, providing exactly the unbounded nested memory needed. CFL = PDA-recognizable, just as Regular = DFA-recognizable.

Context-free grammars

A context-free grammar (CFG) is a tuple (V, Σ, R, S):

CFG — FORMAL DEFINITION
V: finite set of nonterminals (uppercase letters by convention).
Σ: alphabet of terminals (the actual symbols appearing in strings).
R: set of production rules of the form A → α, where A ∈ V and α ∈ (V ∪ Σ)*.
S ∈ V: start symbol.

Strings in the language are derivable from S by repeatedly replacing nonterminals using R, until only terminals remain.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Balanced parentheses

L = { matched paren strings: ε, (), (()), ()(), (()()), ... }

1
Grammar: S → ε  |  (S)  |  SS
2
Derive "(())": S → (S) → ((S)) → (()).
3
Derive "()()": S → SS → (S)S → ()S → ()(S) → ()().
✓
This language is NOT regular but IS context-free.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — { 0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0 }

Grammar: S → ε  |  0S1.
2
Derive "0011": S → 0S1 → 00S11 → 0011.
✓
This is the canonical example of a CFL that is NOT regular.

Derivations and parse trees

A derivation records the substitution steps. A parse tree represents the derivation visually: root is the start symbol; children are the right-hand side of the production applied; leaves are terminals.

📊 FIGURE — A derivation tree for the grammar S → (S)S | ε
Each internal node applies one production; reading the leaves left-to-right yields the derived string "()". Context-free grammars generate exactly the nested, balanced structures that finite automata cannot check — matching parentheses is THE canonical example.

Ambiguity

A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two or more distinct parse trees.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Ambiguous expression grammar

Grammar: E → E + E | E · E | id.

1
Parse "a + b · c" two ways: (a + b) · c, or a + (b · c). Two parse trees → ambiguous.
2
Standard fix: introduce levels for precedence. E → T + E | T; T → F · T | F; F → id.
✓
The new grammar is unambiguous: "a + b · c" forces a + (b · c) by structure.
AMBIGUITY FACTS
Some context-free languages are inherently ambiguous: every grammar for them is ambiguous.

Determining whether a CFG is ambiguous is undecidable in general — no algorithm exists.

In practice, we work with carefully-designed unambiguous grammars (like LR-grammars used by parser generators).

Pushdown automata

A pushdown automaton (PDA) is a finite automaton plus a stack. Each transition reads an input symbol (or ε), pops a stack symbol (or doesn't), and pushes a string of stack symbols.

PDA — KEY IDEA
Tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, Z₀, F):
Γ: stack alphabet.
Z₀: initial stack symbol.
δ: transition based on (state, input symbol or ε, top of stack).

Acceptance: end in F (acceptance by final state), OR empty stack (acceptance by empty stack). Both are equivalent for general PDAs.

PDAs ↔ CFGs

CFL ↔ PDA EQUIVALENCE
A language is context-free iff it is recognized by some PDA.

Construction in either direction is mechanical: PDA from CFG (rules guide the stack manipulation), or CFG from PDA.

Closure properties of context-free languages

CFLS ARE CLOSED UNDER:
Union: ✓   Concatenation: ✓   Kleene star: ✓

NOT closed under:
• Intersection (CFL ∩ CFL is generally not a CFL)
• Complement (Σ* \\ CFL is generally not a CFL)

This is in contrast to regular languages, which are closed under all these operations.

Pumping lemma for CFLs

There's a CFL pumping lemma — more elaborate than the regular version, used to prove a language is NOT context-free.

PUMPING LEMMA FOR CFLS
If L is context-free, there exists a pumping length p such that any w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p can be written as w = uvxyz with:
1. |vy| ≥ 1 (v and y are not both empty);
2. |vxy| ≤ p;
3. for all i ≥ 0, u · vⁱ · x · yⁱ · z ∈ L.

Used to prove e.g. {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is NOT context-free.

Chomsky normal form

Every CFG can be converted to Chomsky Normal Form (CNF): rules are either A → BC (two nonterminals on the right) or A → a (one terminal). CNF is used by parsing algorithms like CYK.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Confusing CFG with regex. CFGs are strictly more powerful: they handle nested patterns; regex (and DFAs) cannot.

Thinking CFLs are closed under intersection. They are NOT — intersection of two CFLs may not be a CFL.

Believing all balanced-pattern languages are context-free. {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is NOT context-free, despite looking similar to {aⁿbⁿ}.

Confusing PDA acceptance modes. Final-state and empty-stack are equivalent in expressive power but produce different sets of recognizing PDAs.

Calling a grammar ambiguous because it allows multiple DERIVATIONS. The criterion is multiple PARSE TREES, not derivations — different derivations can correspond to the same parse tree.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Is L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ} context-free?" — yes, with grammar S → ε | 0S1.

"Construct a CFG for ..." — design recursion that builds the structure.

"What is a parse tree?" — tree showing how the grammar derives a string.

"PDA = ?" — finite automaton + stack = recognizes context-free languages.

"Are CFLs closed under intersection?" — NO.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • CFG: productions A → α, where A is a single nonterminal.
  • Parse tree: visualizes the derivation of a string from the grammar.
  • Ambiguous grammar: some string has two or more parse trees.
  • PDA: finite automaton plus a stack; recognizes exactly the CFLs.
  • CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, Kleene star — but NOT intersection or complement.
  • {aⁿbⁿ} is context-free; {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is NOT.
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A context-free grammar (CFG) has productions like A → αβ and generates the context-free languages (a superset of regular) — e.g., balanced parentheses aⁿbⁿ, which no DFA can do. OA: recognize CFGs are more powerful than finite automata.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
S -> aSb | e     generates a^n b^n
'', 'ab', 'aabb', 'aaabbb', ...

Result: CFG handles aⁿbⁿ (DFA cannot)

Context-free grammars add a stack's worth of memory (via recursion), letting them match nested/balanced structure that regular languages cannot.

📚 Extra review — 1 alternate explanation & recall cards (tap to open)

📜 Context-Free Grammars

TerminalActual alphabet character — final outputa, b

WORKED EXAMPLE — derive "aabb" from S → aSb | ε
StepApplyString

2S → aSbaaSbb
3S → εaabb ✓
Every derivation adds one a on the left AND one b on the right → the language is aⁿbⁿ (equal counts, a's first).
WHY CFGs MATTER
aⁿbⁿ is NOT regular — no DFA can count unboundedly. CFGs are strictly MORE powerful than regex/DFAs: they handle nesting (matched parentheses, HTML tags, programming-language syntax).
⚠️ POWER LADDER SO FAR
Regular (DFA/regex) ⊂ Context-free (grammars/pushdown). Balanced/nested structure → you need at least a CFG.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
The grammar S → aSb | ε generates which language?
  1. aⁿbⁿ — equal a's then equal b's
  2. All strings of a's and b's
  3. Alternating ab's
  4. Only "ab"
Show answer + steps
A. Each rule use wraps the middle with one a…b pair; ε stops it → n a's followed by n b's.

📖 Learn it step by step — Turing Machines & Computability

A Turing machine is the most powerful abstract computer: a finite control plus an infinite tape it can read, write, and move along. It captures everything that is computable — if a Turing machine can’t solve a problem, no computer can.

THE BIG IDEAS
• Church-Turing thesis: “computable” means “computable by a Turing machine.” All reasonable models of computation are equivalent in power.
• Decidable problem = some Turing machine always halts with a yes/no answer.
• Undecidable problem = no algorithm can solve it for all inputs. These exist!
• The Halting Problem — “will this program halt on this input?” — is the famous undecidable problem. No general algorithm can decide it.
📊 FIGURE — A Turing machine mid-computation
An infinite tape of cells, a head that reads/writes one cell and moves left or right, and a finite control state — that is the whole machine, yet it captures everything computable. The halting problem asks whether a given machine ever stops: provably undecidable.
WORKED EXAMPLE — why the Halting Problem is undecidable (the idea)
Suppose a machine H could decide halting. Build a trickster machine D that asks H “do I halt?” and then does the opposite — loops forever if H says halt, halts if H says loop. Ask “does D halt on itself?” Either answer contradicts what D does. The contradiction proves H can’t exist. (This is a proof by contradiction / diagonalization.)
P vs NP (a related complexity idea)
• P = problems solvable quickly (polynomial time). NP = problems whose answers are quickly checkable. Whether P = NP is the famous open question. Undecidability is about “solvable at all”; P vs NP is about “solvable efficiently.”
⚠️ UNDECIDABLE ≠ HARD-BUT-DOABLE
Undecidable means no algorithm exists, ever, not “slow” or “we haven’t found one.” Don’t confuse it with NP-hard problems, which can be solved (just maybe slowly). The Halting Problem can never be solved in general, at any speed.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
The Halting Problem is:
  1. Undecidable — no algorithm solves it for all inputs
  2. Solvable but slow
  3. Regular
Show answer
A. It is undecidable: no general algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary program halts on an arbitrary input.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Turing machine is the universal model of computation: anything any computer can compute, a Turing machine can compute (Church-Turing thesis). Studying Turing machines reveals two profound truths: most languages are not computable at all (the set of all languages is uncountable; the set of TM-recognizable languages is countable), and even among the recognizable ones, many problems are undecidable — provably impossible to solve algorithmically. The famous halting problem is the prototypical example. This is the deepest layer of theoretical CS, and the OA tests recognition of the Chomsky hierarchy and the major undecidable problems.

The Turing machine

A Turing machine (TM) has a finite control plus an infinite read/write tape. At each step, it reads the symbol under the head, writes a symbol, moves left or right, and transitions to a new state.

TURING MACHINE — FORMAL DEFINITION
Tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, q_accept, q_reject):
Q: finite set of states.
Σ: input alphabet.
Γ ⊇ Σ: tape alphabet (includes a blank symbol □).
δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}. Read a symbol, write a symbol, move left or right, change state.
q₀: start state.
q_accept, q_reject: distinguished accepting/rejecting states.

Computation halts when entering q_accept or q_reject. May also run forever (loop).

Recognizable vs. decidable

The two key classes of languages with respect to Turing machines:

RECOGNIZABLE VS. DECIDABLE
Turing-recognizable (also "recursively enumerable" or "RE"): some TM accepts every string in L. On strings NOT in L, the TM may loop forever (no need to halt).

Turing-decidable (also "recursive"): some TM that halts on EVERY input — accepting strings in L, rejecting strings not in L.

Decidable ⊂ Recognizable. The famous "halting problem" is recognizable but not decidable.

The Chomsky hierarchy

CHOMSKY HIERARCHY
Four nested classes of formal languages:

Type 3 — Regular: recognized by DFA / NFA. Described by regex.
Type 2 — Context-free: recognized by PDA. Generated by CFG.
Type 1 — Context-sensitive: recognized by linear-bounded TM. Generated by context-sensitive grammar.
Type 0 — Recursively enumerable: recognized by general TM. Generated by unrestricted grammar.

Each strictly contains the one below: Regular ⊊ CFL ⊊ CSL ⊊ RE.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Where does each language sit?
1
L = {strings of even length}: Regular (DFA with 2 states).
2
L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ}: CFL but not regular (CFG: S → ε | 0S1).
3
L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ2ⁿ}: Context-sensitive but not CFL (need to count three things; PDA can't).
4
L = {⟨M⟩ : M is a TM that accepts ε}: RE but not decidable (you can simulate, but it might loop).

The Church-Turing thesis

CHURCH-TURING THESIS
Anything computable by any reasonable model of computation is computable by a Turing machine.

This is a thesis (philosophical claim), not a theorem — it captures our intuition about what "algorithm" means. All known models — λ-calculus, RAM machines, partial recursive functions, modern programming languages — are TM-equivalent.

The halting problem

The most famous undecidability result. Asks: given a Turing machine M and input w, does M halt on w?

HALTING PROBLEM
HALT = { ⟨M, w⟩ : Turing machine M halts on input w }

Theorem (Turing, 1936): HALT is recognizable but NOT decidable.

Consequence: no algorithm can correctly decide, for every program and input, whether the program will halt.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Proof sketch (diagonalization)
1
Suppose H(M, w) decides whether M halts on w. Build D as: D(⟨M⟩) = "if H(M, ⟨M⟩) says halts, loop forever; else halt."
2
Now run D(⟨D⟩). If D halts on ⟨D⟩, then D loops on ⟨D⟩ — contradiction. If D loops, D halts — contradiction.
3
So no such H can exist. The halting problem is undecidable.

Reductions and undecidability

To prove a problem P is undecidable, reduce the halting problem (or another known undecidable problem) to P. If you could decide P, you could decide HALT — contradiction.

CLASSIC UNDECIDABLE PROBLEMS
Halting problem: does TM M halt on w?
Acceptance: does TM M accept w?
Emptiness: is L(M) = ∅?
Equivalence: do TMs M₁ and M₂ accept the same language?
Post Correspondence Problem (PCP).
Rice's theorem: any nontrivial property of TM languages is undecidable. (E.g., "M accepts at least one even-length string" is undecidable.)

Decidable problems for small classes

Many problems undecidable for general TMs become decidable for restricted machines:

DECIDABILITY BY LANGUAGE CLASS
For DFAs, NFAs, regex (regular):
• Membership, emptiness, equivalence, ALL decidable.

For CFGs/PDAs (context-free):
• Membership: decidable (via CYK algorithm).
• Emptiness: decidable.
• Equivalence: UNDECIDABLE. ← surprising.

For Turing machines:
• Membership/halting: undecidable.
• Most nontrivial questions: undecidable (Rice's theorem).

Complexity classes (brief preview)

Among decidable problems, complexity theory studies how efficiently they can be solved.

P, NP, AND BEYOND
P: decidable in polynomial time.
NP: verifiable in polynomial time. (Solutions, when given, are checkable in polynomial time.)
NP-complete: the hardest problems in NP. SAT, 3-SAT, Hamilton cycle, vertex cover.

P vs NP question: Are these the same class? Open since 1971. Most believe P ≠ NP, but no proof.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Confusing recognizable with decidable. Decidable ⇒ recognizable. The halting problem is recognizable but NOT decidable.

Thinking the Chomsky hierarchy strictly nests by syntax rather than expressive power. Each class of grammars (regular, CFG, CSG, unrestricted) corresponds to a different language class — and each strictly grows.

Believing modern computers are more powerful than Turing machines. They are formally equivalent (Church-Turing thesis). Real computers have finite memory and are less powerful in theory.

Misunderstanding undecidability. "Undecidable" doesn't mean "hard" — it means provably impossible by any algorithm.

Calling NP "non-polynomial." It stands for "Nondeterministic Polynomial," meaning verifiable in polynomial time.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Is the halting problem decidable?" — NO, but it is recognizable.

"Chomsky hierarchy from least to most powerful?" — Regular ⊊ CFL ⊊ CSL ⊊ RE.

"Difference between recognizable and decidable?" — decidable TMs always halt; recognizable may loop on rejections.

"Church-Turing thesis says ...?" — anything computable is computable by a Turing machine.

"NP stands for ...?" — Nondeterministic Polynomial time.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • A Turing machine has a finite control + infinite tape; the universal model of computation.
  • Decidable ⊂ recognizable: decidable means always halts; recognizable allows looping on rejects.
  • Chomsky hierarchy: Regular ⊊ Context-free ⊊ Context-sensitive ⊊ Recursively enumerable.
  • Halting problem is recognizable but NOT decidable (Turing 1936).
  • Rice's theorem: every nontrivial semantic property of TM languages is undecidable.
  • Church-Turing thesis: all reasonable computational models are TM-equivalent.
  • P, NP, NP-complete: complexity classes within decidable problems.
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A Turing machine (infinite tape) is the model of general computation; the Church-Turing thesis says it captures 'computable'. The halting problem is UNDECIDABLE — no algorithm decides if an arbitrary program halts. OA: TM is most powerful; halting is undecidable.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
hierarchy: regular < context-free < ... < Turing-recognizable
halting problem: provably no general decider

Result: Turing machines = general computation; halting undecidable

Turing machines sit atop the Chomsky hierarchy; the halting problem's undecidability is the canonical limit of computation the OA references.

📚 Extra review — 1 alternate explanation & recall cards (tap to open)

♾️ Turing Machines & Computability

TermDefinition
Turing machineAn infinite tape + a read/write head + states — the mathematical model of ANY computer
Church-Turing thesisAnything computable at all is computable by a Turing machine

Undecidable problemNO algorithm can solve every instance — proven impossible, not just hard
THE HALTING PROBLEM (the famous one)
"Given any program and input, will it eventually halt?" — UNDECIDABLE. Turing proved no algorithm can answer this for ALL programs (a self-reference/diagonal argument: feed the supposed halt-checker a program built to contradict it).
WORKED EXAMPLE — classify each
ProblemStatus
"Is this number even?"Decidable (trivially)
"Does this string match this regex?"Decidable
"Does this program halt on this input?"Undecidable
THE FULL POWER LADDER
Regular ⊂ Context-free ⊂ Decidable ⊂ Recognizable — each level can do everything below it, plus more.
⚠️ UNDECIDABLE ≠ "REALLY HARD"
NP-complete problems (like SAT) are slow but SOLVABLE. Undecidable problems are IMPOSSIBLE for any algorithm, ever. Different categories entirely.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
The Halting Problem is:
  1. Undecidable — no algorithm solves all cases
  2. Decidable but slow
  3. NP-complete
  4. Solvable with enough memory
Show answer + steps
A. Turing's proof shows a universal halt-checker is self-contradictory — impossibility, not difficulty.

The inclusion-exclusion principle

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When you count things in overlapping groups, adding the group sizes double-counts whatever is in the overlap. Inclusion-exclusion fixes this: add the sizes, then subtract the overlaps you counted twice.

📊 FIGURE — Inclusion–exclusion with real counts
|A| = 12 and |B| = 9 both count the 4 elements of the overlap — adding them double-counts it. Subtract it back once: |A ∪ B| = 12 + 9 − 4 = 17. With three sets the pattern continues: add singles, subtract pairs, add back the triple.
TWO SETS
|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. You include both sets, then exclude the intersection counted twice.
THREE SETS
|A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A|+|B|+|C| − |A∩B| − |A∩C| − |B∩C| + |A∩B∩C|. Singles add, pairs subtract, the triple adds back.
WORKED EXAMPLE — two sets

In a class of 30: 18 take Math, 15 take Physics, 7 take both. How many take at least one?

|M ∪ P| = 18 + 15 − 7 = 26. (Subtracting the 7 fixes the double-count.)

📝 EXAM WORDING

Include the individual sets, exclude the pairwise overlaps, then (for 3 sets) add back the triple overlap. The alternating +/−/+ pattern generalizes to any number of sets. Watch for "at least one" (the union) vs "exactly one."

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
40 people: 25 like coffee, 20 like tea, 10 like both. How many like at least one?
  1. 45
  2. 35
  3. 30
  4. 55
Show answer
B. 25 + 20 − 10 = 35.

Why the signs alternate

Inclusion–exclusion answers one question: how many things are in at least one of these sets? Adding the sizes overcounts anything that sits in more than one, so you correct — and the correction itself overcorrects, so you correct the correction.

📊 FIGURE — two sets: add, then remove the double-count
📘 DEFINITION

Two sets: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|

Three sets: |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A∩B| − |A∩C| − |B∩C| + |A∩B∩C|

In general: add all the singles, subtract all the pairs, add all the triples, subtract all the quadruples — the sign of a k-way intersection is (−1)k+1.

📊 FIGURE — three sets, and what happens to the centre

Track one element to see why it works. An item in all three sets is counted 3 times by the singles, removed 3 times by the pairs, leaving 0 — so the +|A∩B∩C| brings it to exactly 1. An item in exactly two sets is counted twice, removed once by its one pair, and is untouched by the triple: 1. An item in one set: 1. Every element ends up counted exactly once, which is what a union count means.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — 120 students; 60 take French, 50 take German, 45 take Spanish; 20 take French and German, 15 French and Spanish, 12 German and Spanish; 5 take all three. How many take at least one?

|F ∪ G ∪ S| = (60 + 50 + 45) − (20 + 15 + 12) + 5

= 155 − 47 + 5 = 113.

So 120 − 113 = 7 take no language at all. The follow-up question is almost always that complement, so compute it while the numbers are in front of you.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — how many students take exactly one language?

Work outward from the centre. French only = 60 − 20 − 15 + 5 = 30. German only = 50 − 20 − 12 + 5 = 23. Spanish only = 45 − 15 − 12 + 5 = 23.

Exactly one = 30 + 23 + 23 = 76.

Check against the total: exactly two = (20−5) + (15−5) + (12−5) = 32, exactly three = 5, so 76 + 32 + 5 = 113 ✓ — the union we already computed.

The +5 in each "only" line is not optional: subtracting both pairwise overlaps removes the triple-overlap students twice, so they must be added back.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

"20 take French and German" almost always means at least those two, i.e. the whole lens including the students who also take Spanish. If a problem instead says "exactly two", the numbers are the disjoint regions and you must not subtract again. Read which one you were given before writing anything down — the two readings give different answers and both are on the option list.

📘 DEFINITION

The complement form is often shorter. To count items with none of the properties:

N(none) = N − |A| − |B| − |C| + |A∩B| + |A∩C| + |B∩C| − |A∩B∩C|

which is just N minus the union, with every sign flipped.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — how many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by none of 2, 3 or 5?
SetCount
div by 2⌊100/2⌋ = 50
div by 3⌊100/3⌋ = 33
div by 5⌊100/5⌋ = 20
div by 6⌊100/6⌋ = 16the 2-and-3 overlap
div by 10⌊100/10⌋ = 10the 2-and-5 overlap
div by 15⌊100/15⌋ = 6the 3-and-5 overlap
div by 30⌊100/30⌋ = 3all three

Union = (50 + 33 + 20) − (16 + 10 + 6) + 3 = 103 − 32 + 3 = 74.

So divisible by none = 100 − 74 = 26.

The pairwise overlaps are the multiples of the least common multiples — 6, 10, 15 — not of the products. For 2 and 3 they coincide, but for a pair like 4 and 6 they do not: lcm(4,6) = 12, while 4 × 6 = 24 would undercount.

📘 DEFINITION

A derangement is a permutation leaving no element in its original position, and counting them is inclusion–exclusion applied to "the ith item is fixed":

D(n) = n! [1 − 1/1! + 1/2! − 1/3! + … + (−1)ⁿ/n!]

D(1) = 0, D(2) = 1, D(3) = 2, D(4) = 9, D(5) = 44. The proportion D(n)/n! converges to 1/e ≈ 0.368 — so about 37% of shuffles leave nothing in place, whatever the size.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Three signals that a question wants inclusion–exclusion: the word "or" joining conditions that can hold together; the phrase "at least one"; and any question asking for "none", which is the complement of exactly that union. If the conditions were mutually exclusive you would just add, and the problem would not have bothered giving you overlaps.

Modular Arithmetic, CRT & RSA

Congruence a ≡ b (mod m) means m | (a−b). Fast exponentiation reduces at every step: compute a^k mod m by repeated squaring.

⚙️ FORMULAS
  • Fermat: if p prime and p∤a, then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
  • Euler φ: for n=pq, φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1).
  • RSA: pick e with gcd(e,φ)=1; private d ≡ e⁻¹ (mod φ); encrypt c=m^e mod n; decrypt m=c^d mod n.
  • Bézout: gcd(a,b)=as+bt via the extended Euclidean algorithm.

Counting

💡 KEY RESULTS
  • Permutations P(n,r)=n!/(n−r)!; combinations C(n,r)=n!/(r!(n−r)!).
  • Stars & bars: nonnegative solutions of x₁+…+x_k=n is C(n+k−1,k−1).
  • Inclusion–exclusion: |A∪B∪C| = Σ|A| − Σ|A∩B| + |A∩B∩C|.
  • Pigeonhole: n items in k boxes force some box to hold ⌈n/k⌉.

Recurrences & Induction

📝 TECHNIQUE

Linear homogeneous a_n=c₁a_{n−1}+c₂a_{n−2}: solve characteristic x²=c₁x+c₂; distinct roots give a_n=Ar₁ⁿ+Br₂ⁿ. For a_n=ca_{n−1}+f(n), add a particular solution to the homogeneous one, then fit constants to initial values.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Strong induction assumes the claim for all k<n, not just n−1; prime-factorization and recurrence proofs need that full hypothesis. Also verify enough base cases to cover the recurrence's depth.

Conditional Probability & Bayes

⚙️ FORMULAS
  • P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B).
  • Bayes: P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H) / Σ P(E|Hᵢ)P(Hᵢ).
  • Expectation: E[X]=Σ x·P(X=x); linearity E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y] always holds.

📝 TECHNIQUE

For "expected count" problems use indicator variables: X=ΣIᵢ, so E[X]=Σ P(Iᵢ=1) even when the Iᵢ are dependent. This gives fixed-points-of-a-permutation =1 instantly.

💡 KEY RESULTS

📝 TECHNIQUE

A DFA/NFA recognizes a language iff it is regular (equivalently describable by a regular expression). NFAs allow ε-moves and multiple transitions but recognize the same class as DFAs.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

The pumping lemma proves non-regularity: for regular L there is a length p so every long w=xyz (|xy|≤p, |y|≥1) has all xyⁱz∈L. Languages needing unbounded counting — {aⁿbⁿ}, balanced parentheses, {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} — fail this and are not regular; finite languages are always regular.

Formulas & method

Euclid's algorithm: repeatedly replace (a,b) with (b, a mod b) until the remainder is 0; the last nonzero value is gcd. Example: gcd(48,36): 48 = 1·36 + 12, then 36 = 3·12 + 0, so gcd = 12.

Modular exponentiation: to get a^b mod m, reduce as you multiply. Example: 3^5 mod 7. Powers of 3 mod 7: 3, 9≡2, 6, 18≡4, 12≡5, so 3^5 ≡ 5.

Linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod m): find the inverse of a mod m, then x ≡ a⁻¹·b. For 3x ≡ 4 (mod 5), since 3·2 = 6 ≡ 1, the inverse is 2, so x ≡ 2·4 = 8 ≡ 3 (mod 5). Check: 3·3 = 9 ≡ 4. ✓

Counting

  • Permutations (order matters): P(n,r) = n!/(n−r)!. P(6,2) = 6·5 = 30.
  • Combinations (order ignored): C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!). C(7,3) = 35.
  • Arrangements with repeats: n! divided by the factorial of each repeated letter's count.
  • Subsets of an n-element set: 2ⁿ.

Pigeonhole principle: with k boxes, you need k+1 objects to guarantee two share a box. With 12 months, 13 people guarantee a shared birth month.

Formulas & method

Basic probability: P(event) = favorable outcomes / total outcomes. Drawing one card, P(heart) = 13/52 = 1/4.

Expected value: E[X] = Σ x·P(x). A fair die: (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5.

Bayes' theorem: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) / [P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|Aᶜ)P(Aᶜ)]. If P(A)=0.5, P(B|A)=0.8, P(B|Aᶜ)=0.4, then P(A|B) = (0.4)/(0.4+0.2) = 2/3.

Recurrences

  • Evaluate step by step: for a(n) = a(n−1) + 2n with a(0)=1: a(1)=3, a(2)=7, a(3)=13.
  • Closed form of a geometric recurrence: a(n) = c·a(n−1), a(0)=k gives a(n) = k·cⁿ. For a(n)=2a(n−1), a(0)=3: a(n)=3·2ⁿ, so a(5)=3·32=96.

Product rule: if step 1 has n₁ choices and step 2 has n₂ choices, together they have n₁·n₂. With repetition allowed, a length-3 string over 26 letters has 26³ = 17576 possibilities.

Drawing without replacement: use combinations. From 3 red and 2 blue, P(both red in a draw of 2) = C(3,2)/C(5,2) = 3/10.

Core formulas & methods

The Euclidean algorithm finds gcd(a,b) by repeated division: replace (a,b) with (b, a mod b) until the remainder is 0; the last nonzero remainder is the gcd. Then lcm(a,b) = a·b / gcd(a,b).

Modular arithmetic

For modular exponentiation a^b mod m, reduce as you go and use cycles: if a^k ≡ 1 (mod m), then a^b ≡ a^(b mod k). Products reduce too: (a·b) mod m = ((a mod m)·(b mod m)) mod m.

A modular inverse a^(-1) mod m is the x with a·x ≡ 1 (mod m); it exists exactly when gcd(a,m)=1. To solve a linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod m), multiply both sides by a^(-1): x ≡ a^(-1)·b (mod m).

CRT and totients

The Chinese Remainder Theorem combines x ≡ r₁ (mod m₁) and x ≡ r₂ (mod m₂) with coprime moduli into a unique solution mod m₁·m₂; for small systems just scan one residue class. Euler's totient φ(n) counts integers up to n coprime to n: for n = p₁^e₁···p_k^e_k, φ(n) = n·∏(1 − 1/pᵢ).

Worked example: Compute 2^10 mod 11. Since 2^10 = 1024 = 93·11 + 1, the answer is 1 (matching Fermat's little theorem, since 11 is prime).

Counting work & growth rates

Binary search halves the range each step, so its worst case is ⌈log₂ n⌉ comparisons; linear search takes up to n comparisons. This gap explains why sorted-array search is fast.

Loop counting

Count exactly by summing. A loop whose inner body runs i times for i = 1…n executes Σ i = n(n+1)/2 times. Three independent nested loops from 1 to n run n³ times. Insertion or bubble sort makes up to n(n−1)/2 comparisons in the worst case, and bubble-sort swaps equal the number of inversions.

Recurrences & the Master Theorem

For T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n), compare f(n) with n^(log_b a):

  • If f is polynomially smaller, T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)) (Case 1).
  • If f = Θ(n^(log_b a)), T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)·log n) (Case 2).
  • If f is polynomially larger (with regularity), T(n) = Θ(f(n)) (Case 3).

Growth ordering

From slowest to fastest: log n, n, n log n, n², 2^n, n!. When ranking, the fastest-growing dominates for large n.

Worked example: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n we have a = b = 2, so n^(log₂ 2) = n = f(n); Case 2 gives Θ(n log n).

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

📋 Advanced Graph Theory

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Graph coloring and chromatic number

⚠ GREEDY BOUND Greedy coloring never needs more than Δ + 1 colors (Δ = max degree). It's an upper bound — the true χ may be smaller.

Planarity and Euler's formula

▸ EULER’S FORMULA (the one equation) For any connected planar graph drawn without crossings: V − E + F = 2 , where V = vertices, E = edges, and F = faces (regions), including the one big outer region . Always remember to count that outer face.

▸ TESTS FOR NON-PLANARITY • Edge bound: a simple connected planar graph with V ≥ 3 has E ≤ 3V − 6 . If a graph breaks this, it is not planar . • Two famous non-planar graphs: K₅ (5 vertices all connected) and K₃,₃ (the “three utilities” graph). Kuratowski’s theorem: a graph is non-planar exactly when…

▸ EULER'S FORMULA (connected planar graph) v − e + f = 2

▸ PLANARITY TESTS Simple planar with v ≥ 3: e ≤ 3v − 6 . The two famous NON-planar graphs: K₅ (e=10 > 3·5−6=9) and K₃,₃ . Kuratowski: a graph is non-planar ⟺ it contains a K₅ or K₃,₃ "shape" inside it.

⚠ COUNT THE OUTER FACE The single most common Euler-formula mistake is forgetting the unbounded outer region as a face. And the E ≤ 3V − 6 bound only disproves planarity when broken — passing it doesn’t guarantee…

⚠ DON'T FORGET THE OUTER FACE A triangle drawn on paper has f = 2: the inside AND the unbounded outside region.

Eulerian and Hamiltonian paths

▸ THE DEFINITIONS + THE EULER TEST • Eulerian circuit = a closed tour using every edge exactly once . Test: the graph is connected and every vertex has even degree . • Eulerian path (open, not closed): exists when exactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree . (If 2 odd, the path must start at one and end…

▸ THE EULER DEGREE TEST (connected graph) Euler CIRCUIT (ends where it starts): ALL vertices have EVEN degree. Euler PATH (different endpoints): EXACTLY 2 vertices have odd degree (they're the endpoints). More than 2 odd vertices → neither exists.

▸ HAMILTONIAN SUFFICIENT CONDITION (Dirac) If every vertex has degree ≥ n/2 (n ≥ 3), a Hamiltonian circuit EXISTS. (It's sufficient, not necessary — cycles fail Dirac yet are Hamiltonian.)

⚠ EULER = EVEN DEGREES; HAMILTON HAS NO EASY TEST Don’t invent a degree rule for Hamiltonian circuits — there isn’t a clean one. The counting shortcut (all-even → Euler circuit; exactly two odd → Euler path) applies…

⚠ EDGE vs VERTEX — READ THE QUESTION "Every edge once" → Euler. "Every vertex once" → Hamiltonian. Half the OA points on this topic are just this distinction.

Network flows and matching

▸ THE KEY RULES & THEOREM • Capacity: flow on an edge can’t exceed its capacity. • Conservation: at every vertex except s and t, flow in = flow out (nothing is created or lost). • A cut splits the vertices into s’s side and t’s side; its capacity is the total capacity of edges crossing from s-side to…

▸ MAX-FLOW MIN-CUT THEOREM maximum flow = minimum cut capacity — the tightest bottleneck decides everything.

⚠ FLOW IS LIMITED BY THE SMALLEST CUT Max flow is never bigger than any cut, so the minimum cut pins it exactly. When you’re asked for max flow, hunt for the tightest bottleneck — you don’t have to trace every path if you can spot one cut whose capacity everything must squeeze through — that cut's capacity IS the max flow.

📋 Trees and Spanning Trees

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Tree properties and traversals

▸ SHARPER TREE FACTS • A tree on n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges and is maximally acyclic / minimally connected (add any edge → a cycle; drop any edge → disconnected). • A tree with at least 2 vertices has at least two leaves . • Cayley’s formula: the number of distinct labeled trees on n vertices…

▸ BINARY TREE CAPACITY Height h: level i holds ≤ 2ⁱ nodes; the whole tree holds ≤ 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes.

⚠ HEIGHT DRIVES SEARCH COST, NOT TRAVERSAL COST Visiting all nodes is always O(n). But searching a binary search tree costs O(height): O(log n) when balanced, but O(n) if it degenerated into a line. Balance is what…

⚠ BFS ≠ DFS BFS (queue) explores level by level; DFS (stack/recursion) dives deep first — pre/in/postorder are all DFS variants.

Spanning trees and MST algorithms

▸ THE TWO CORRECTNESS RULES • Cut property: for any way of splitting the vertices into two groups, the cheapest edge crossing the split is in some MST . (This is why Prim’s greedy choice is safe.) • Cycle property: for any cycle, the most expensive edge on that cycle is NOT in any MST (unless tied).…

▸ RECAP + THE CUT PROPERTY Spanning tree: touches every vertex, n − 1 edges. MST = minimum total weight. Cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut is ALWAYS in some MST — it's why greedy (Kruskal/Prim) works.

⚠ MST MINIMIZES TOTAL WEIGHT, NOT PATH LENGTH An MST gives the cheapest way to connect everything ; it does not guarantee the shortest path between two specific vertices (that’s Dijkstra’s job). Don’t use an MST to…

⚠ UNIQUE WEIGHTS → UNIQUE MST If all edge weights differ, the MST is unique. With ties, several MSTs may share the same minimum total.

Permutations and combinations

▸ THE TWO FORMULAS • Permutation (order matters): P(n, k) = n! / (n − k)!. (arrangements — 1st, 2nd, 3rd are different roles) • Combination (order does NOT matter): C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n − k)!). (a group/committee — just who’s in it) Same as permutations but divided by k! to erase the orderings you…

⚠ ASK “DOES ORDER MATTER?” FIRST Roles, rankings, sequences, passwords, seat arrangements → permutation . Teams, committees, hands of cards, subsets → combination . Using P where you need C over-counts by a factor of…

▸ THE TWO FORMS • Basic: if n items go into m boxes and n > m, at least one box has ≥ 2 items. • Generalized: with n items in m boxes, at least one box has ≥ ⌈n/m⌉ items (round up ). This is the version most problems need.

▸ BASIC FORM Put n + 1 pigeons into n holes → some hole holds AT LEAST 2. Generalized: n items in k boxes → some box holds at least ⌈n / k⌉ .

▸ THE ONE FORMULA THAT UNLOCKS IT The geometric series identity is the workhorse: 1 + x + x² + x³ + … = 1/(1 − x) (for |x| < 1). So the sequence 1, 1, 1, 1, … is “stored” as the tidy function 1/(1−x). Variations: 1/(1−ax) stores 1, a, a², … and 1/(1−x)² stores 1, 2, 3, 4, …

▸ THE IDEA Encode a counting sequence a₀, a₁, a₂, … as the coefficients of a power series: G(x) = a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + … Multiply/manipulate the algebra → read answers off the coefficients.

⚠ THE EXPONENT IS THE “AMOUNT,” THE COEFFICIENT IS THE “COUNT” Keep the roles straight: x’s power encodes the total (size, cents, items chosen); the number in front is how many ways to reach that total. The point of…

▸ SOLVING LINEAR HOMOGENEOUS RECURRENCES (the method) For aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂: 1) write the characteristic equation r² = c₁r + c₂ · 2) find roots r₁, r₂ · 3) general solution aₙ = A·r₁ⁿ + B·r₂ⁿ · 4) use initial conditions to find A, B.

⚠ YOU NEED THE INITIAL CONDITIONS The characteristic equation gives the form A·r₁ⁿ + B·r₂ⁿ, but A and B are unknown until you plug in the starting values (a₀, a₁). Repeated roots need a special form (A + Bn)rⁿ — don’t…

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Discrete probability

▸ THE BASIC RULES • Range: 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. All outcomes’ probabilities add to 1. • Complement: P(not E) = 1 − P(E). (Often easier to count the opposite.) • Addition (OR): P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Subtract the overlap so it’s not double-counted. • Multiplication (AND, independent): P(A and…

▸ THE THREE CORE RULES Complement: P(A′) = 1 − P(A) · Addition: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) · Range: 0 ≤ P ≤ 1

⚠ SUBTRACT THE OVERLAP FOR “OR” P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) only when A and B are mutually exclusive (can’t both happen). Otherwise you must subtract P(A and B) or you double-count the shared cases. For “AND,” multiplying…

⚠ SUBTRACT THE OVERLAP P(A∪B) without subtracting P(A∩B) double-counts outcomes in both events — the OA's favorite wrong option.

Conditional probability and Bayes

▸ THE TWO FORMULAS • Conditional: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B). (of the B-world, what fraction is also A?) • Bayes’ theorem (flips the condition around): P(A | B) = P(B | A)·P(A) / P(B). Use it when you know P(B | A) but want P(A | B).

▸ THE DEFINITIONS Conditional: P(A|B) = P(A∩B) / P(B) — "probability of A GIVEN B happened." Independent events: P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B) (knowing B tells you nothing about A).

⚠ P(A|B) IS NOT P(B|A) “Probability you’re sick given a positive test” is very different from “probability of a positive test given you’re sick.” Bayes’ theorem is exactly the tool for converting one into the other —…

⚠ P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A) P(spam | WIN) and P(WIN | spam) are different numbers — Bayes exists precisely to convert one into the other.

▸ THE FORMULAS • Expected value: E(X) = Σ [x·P(x)] — multiply each outcome by its probability and add. (A weighted average.) • Variance: Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² — the average of the squares minus the square of the average. • Standard deviation = √Var(X), in the same units as X.

▸ EXPECTED VALUE E[X] = Σ (value × probability) — the long-run average.

▸ VARIANCE — how spread out Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])² · Standard deviation = √Var

⚠ EXPECTED VALUE IS AN AVERAGE, NOT A PREDICTION E(X) = 3.5 doesn’t mean any single roll is 3.5 — it’s the mean over many trials. Two games can share the same expected value but very different variance (risk): one…

▸ THE BIG IDEA PUBLIC key (n, e) encrypts — anyone can use it. PRIVATE key d decrypts — only you have it. Security rests on one fact: factoring a huge n = p·q is computationally infeasible .

The Inclusion-Exclusion Principle

▸ TWO SETS |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. You include both sets, then exclude the intersection counted twice.

▸ THREE SETS |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A|+|B|+|C| − |A∩B| − |A∩C| − |B∩C| + |A∩B∩C|. Singles add, pairs subtract, the triple adds back.

Context-free grammars

▸ THE PIECES OF A GRAMMAR • Terminals = the actual symbols of the language (like a, b, or “+”). • Non-terminals = variables (like S, A) that stand for “something to be expanded.” • Productions = rules like S → aSb (“replace S with aSb”). • Start symbol = where derivations begin (usually S). A string…

▸ THE CHOMSKY HIERARCHY (who’s more powerful) Regular ⊂ Context-free ⊂ Context-sensitive ⊂ Recursively-enumerable. Each level recognizes strictly more languages. Finite automata sit at the bottom (regular); CFGs are the next step up and need a stack (a pushdown automaton) to recognize.

▸ WHY CFGs MATTER aⁿbⁿ is NOT regular — no DFA can count unboundedly. CFGs are strictly MORE powerful than regex/DFAs: they handle nesting (matched parentheses, HTML tags, programming-language syntax).

⚠ CFGs CAN MATCH/NEST, REGEX CANNOT The jump from regular to context-free is exactly the ability to handle balanced/nested structure — matching parentheses, aⁿbⁿ, nested code blocks. If a problem needs counting or…

⚠ POWER LADDER SO FAR Regular (DFA/regex) ⊂ Context-free (grammars/pushdown). Balanced/nested structure → you need at least a CFG.

Turing machines and computability

▸ THE BIG IDEAS • Church-Turing thesis: “computable” means “computable by a Turing machine.” All reasonable models of computation are equivalent in power. • Decidable problem = some Turing machine always halts with a yes/no answer. • Undecidable problem = no algorithm can solve it for all inputs.…

▸ P vs NP (a related complexity idea) • P = problems solvable quickly (polynomial time). NP = problems whose answers are quickly checkable . Whether P = NP is the famous open question. Undecidability is about “solvable at all”; P vs NP is about “solvable efficiently .”

▸ THE HALTING PROBLEM (the famous one) "Given any program and input, will it eventually halt?" — UNDECIDABLE . Turing proved no algorithm can answer this for ALL programs (a self-reference/diagonal argument: feed the supposed halt-checker a program built to contradict it).

▸ THE FULL POWER LADDER Regular ⊂ Context-free ⊂ Decidable ⊂ Recognizable — each level can do everything below it, plus more.

⚠ UNDECIDABLE ≠ HARD-BUT-DOABLE Undecidable means no algorithm exists, ever , not “slow” or “we haven’t found one.” Don’t confuse it with NP-hard problems, which can be solved (just maybe slowly). The Halting Problem…

⚠ UNDECIDABLE ≠ "REALLY HARD" NP-complete problems (like SAT) are slow but SOLVABLE. Undecidable problems are IMPOSSIBLE for any algorithm, ever. Different categories entirely.
